Article Title: Philippines is building 422 MW of solar farms above fish ponds, and the idea could change renewable energy forever
Article Text:
How solar on stilts differs from floating solar

Where the three solar plants will be built

What the companies expect the finished project to deliver

Why the project was announced during a signing witnessed by officials

Why the Philippines is turning to water for solar capacity

What still needs to happen before construction begins

Vietnam's VinEnergo and Philippine developer SunAsia Energy have agreed to build 422 megawatts peak of solar power spread across three sites in the Philippines, using a design that lifts the panels on steel piles above active fish ponds rather than floating them directly on the water. The approach is intended to let fish farming continue underneath the panels without interruption, addressing a conflict over water use and fishing rights that has slowed similar floating solar projects elsewhere in Southeast Asia. VinEnergo is the energy arm of Vietnam's Vingroup, and the deal marks the company's first project in the Philippines.Conventional floating solar setups typically bolt panels onto plastic pontoons that rest directly on the water's surface, shading the water beneath and raising concerns about its effect on aquatic life. According to thejoint announcement from VinEnergo and SunAsia Energy , the system used in this project, described as Solar on Stilts, instead drives steel piles into the pond bed and mounts the panels on top, keeping the water column beneath largely open so boats can pass through and fish farming can continue undisturbed. This rigid, pile-supported structure was also chosen with the Philippines location in mind, since the country sits within the typhoon belt, where a fixed structure driven into the seabed can generally withstand rough weather conditions better than a pontoon based system floating on the surface.The 422 megawatt peak capacity is split across three separate sites. According to solar industry publication PV Tech , the largest plant, at 181 megawatts peak, is planned for Macabebe in Pampanga province north of Manila, while the remaining two plants are located in Negros Occidental in the Visayas region, a 126 megawatt peak site in Sagay and a 115 megawatt peak site in Silay.Together, the three sites will use close to 700,000 solar panels, supported by roughly 62 kilometres of new transmission line built to connect the plants to the grid.According to the same joint announcement from VinEnergo and SunAsia Energy, the companies expect the completed plants to power around 278,000 households once operational and to cut carbon emissions by more than 460,000 tons annually, a figure the companies compare to the equivalent of planting around 21 million trees. The companies also state that the project is expected to generate more than 1.5 billion dollars in lifetime revenue. The deal was signed on June 26 in Hanoi, with VinEnergo CEO Nguyen Anh Khoa and SunAsia CEO and chairperson Tetchi Capellan signing the agreement, and the plants are targeted to come online in 2027 and 2028.The agreement was signed with the Philippines' Energy Secretary Sharon Garin and Vietnam's ambassador to Manila, Lai Thai Binh, both present, according to the joint announcement. The signing also took place while the Philippines was hosting the ASEAN Summit, giving the deal a diplomatic dimension alongside its commercial one. Tetchi Capellan described the model as one where food production and clean energy generation can operate together, according to the companies' own statement, while VinEnergo framed the approach as an extension of its experience in Vietnam protecting local livelihoods while expanding power generation.The Philippines is an archipelago of more than 7,000 islands, and much of its available flat land is already used for agriculture, leaving limited space for utility-scale solar development on land alone. This is not SunAsia's first attempt at combining solar power with existing aquaculture. In 2023, the company and partner BlueLeaf Energy secured rights to develop 1.3 gigawatts of floating solar across Laguna Lake, the country's largest freshwater lake, in a project covering roughly 1,000 hectares that is rolling out in phases toward 2030. The VinEnergo partnership extends this approach beyond a single large lake and into working fish ponds across two separate provinces.As of the signing, construction has not yet started. The agreement marks the beginning of an approximately eighteen-month period covering engineering work, technology selection and contractor arrangements before physical construction is expected to begin, with commissioning targeted for 2027 and 2028. ING advised VinEnergo on the transaction, while SGV and Co. advised SunAsia Energy. Whether the pile-supported design performs as expected at scale across three separate sites, and whether fish farming activity continues smoothly beneath the panels once built, remains to be demonstrated as the project moves from agreement into construction over the coming months.
Article Summary: Vietnam's VinEnergo and Philippine developer SunAsia Energy have agreed to build three solar plants in the Philippines. The plants will use a design that lifts the panels on steel piles above active fish ponds rather than floating them directly on the water. The approach is intended to let fish farming continue underneath the panels without interruption.

Article Title: “We’re told they…”: Candace Owens challenges Andrew Kolvet with ‘retraction’ demand in escalating Charlie Kirk feud
Article Text:
“We’re told they…”: Candace Owens challenges Andrew Kolvet with ‘retraction’ demand in escalating Charlie Kirk feud (Image via Getty)

Candace Owens releases screenshots after Andrew Kolvet questions Daily Mail report

Andrew Kolvet and Candace Owens continue public dispute over Erika Kirk story

The public fight between Candace Owens and Turning Point USA has taken another turn after both sides clashed over a Daily Mail report linked to the 2025 assassination of Charlie Kirk . On July 22, TPUSA spokesman Andrew Kolvet said the organization never received a request for comment before the story was published and questioned whether the article accurately reflected Erika Kirk’s views.Owens pushed back, shared screenshots that she said showed Daily Mail had contacted her team before publication, and challenged Kolvet to seek legal action if he believed the report contained fabricated quotes. The exchange has become the latest chapter in their long-running dispute over Owens’ ongoing coverage of Charlie Kirk’s death.The latest argument began when Andrew Kolvet claimed TPUSA had not received any request for comment from Daily Mail before its story was published.He wrote, “We never received any request for comment. We’re told they attempted to send one, but we can’t find it. Strange given that every other outlet on the planet seems to know how to reach us, including the Daily Mail.”Kolvet also argued that the article did not reflect Erika Kirk’s way of speaking and said the newspaper later made major corrections. He added, “Unfortunate to see the Daily Mail doing the bidding of Candace Owens, who of course used it as rage bait on her show because she has no actual evidence to discuss as she continues her very lucrative ‘investigation.’ Maybe she’s the anonymous source?”Owens responded by saying she doubted Kolvet’s version of events and urged him to demand a correction if it was true.She wrote, “If this is true, and I HIGHLY doubt it is, given its striking similarity to the piece that was being written and spearheaded by Erika’s family friend Tracy Martin for US Magazine, then you should demand a public response and retraction from the Daily Mail.”A short time later, Owens posted screenshots that she said proved her team had received a request for comment before the article went live. She added, “Here you go @AndrewKolvet, please keep us updated on this. We received notice hours before the piece went out, seeking comment.”The back-and-forth did not stop there. Kolvet questioned why Owens had not publicly shared the emails before the article was published. He wrote, “Riddle me this, Candace… We all know what you do when an article is coming out you don’t like. You publish the emails, attack the reporter, and throw a fit on social media. Why didn’t you do that this time? Is it because you were in on the plan? Just asking questions.”Owens rejected the accusation and pointed out that she had already discussed the report on her show.She replied, “I literally did an entire episode responding to this article, genius. Also please stop the ‘just asking questions’ cringe. 😂 You are cornered here. If you are stating that the journalist is fictionalizing quotes from Erika’s family friends, then you should get legal involved. This is an easy retraction to achieve. Quite literally this reporter would lose his job. Are you working on that?”Owens also argued that Daily Mail had corrected only what she described as a typo involving “family friend” and “family member,” not withdrawn the article itself. She maintained that if the quotes were truly invented, TPUSA should pursue a defamation case. As of now, neither side has backed down, and the dispute remains active.
Article Summary: Candace Owens challenges Andrew Kolvet with ‘retraction’ demand in escalating Charlie Kirk feud. TPUSA spokesman Andrew Kolvedt said the organization never received a request for comment before the story was published. Owens pushed back, shared screenshots that she said showed Daily Mail had contacted her team before publication.

Article Title: US, Saudi Arabia sign civil nuclear deal paving way for uranium enrichment
Article Text:
The deal could pave the way for Saudi Arabia to develop uranium enrichment capabilities for its civilian nuclear programme

The United States and Saudi Arabia on Wednesday signed a civil nuclear cooperation agreement that could pave the way for the kingdom to develop uranium enrichment capabilities for its civilian nuclear programme.US Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed the agreement, known as a 123 agreement, along with what the Trump administration described as a bilateral safeguards agreement.While the administration released few details, the framework is expected to allow a joint US-Saudi study on building a uranium enrichment facility in Saudi Arabia. The agreement is expected to remain in force for 30 years and involve US companies in developing the programme."These agreements reflect our two nations' shared commitment to strengthening US-Saudi commercial relations, delivering prosperity at home and security to our allies abroad," Wright said."Rest assured, these agreements uphold the highest standards of nuclear safety and nonproliferation, while relying on the world's best nuclear technology and scientists, designed right here in the United States," he added.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the deal, rejecting concerns that it could fuel nuclear proliferation in the region."The US is not going to reach any agreement with any country in the world that leads to the risk of proliferation," Rubio said.The agreement will now be submitted to the US Congress for review, where it could face opposition from lawmakers concerned that allowing Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium could eventually increase the risk of nuclear weapon development.The announcement comes as the US and Israel continue military operations against Iran, with Washington maintaining that Tehran's uranium enrichment programme could enable it to develop nuclear weapons, a claim Iran denies, insisting its programme is for peaceful purposes.
Article Summary: The deal could pave the way for Saudi Arabia to develop uranium enrichment capabilities for its civilian nuclear programme. The agreement is expected to remain in force for 30 years and involve US companies in developing the programme. It will now be submitted to the US Congress for review, where it could face opposition from lawmakers.

Article Title: D4vd preliminary hearing: Celeste Rivas' family lawyer describes 'gruesome' crime scene photos
Article Text:
Image/X

Celeste Rivas' family lawyer says crime scene photos shown during D4vd hearing were 'gruesome'

Prosecutors outline allegations as D4vd maintains not guilty plea

New details came out during singer D4vd's preliminary hearing as Celeste Rivas' family lawyer spoke about the graphic evidence shown in court. After the hearing, attorney Patrick Steinfeld told TMZ that the crime scene photos were extremely disturbing and very painful for Celeste's family to see. He said the images were so shocking that Celeste's mother cried throughout the hearing. D4vd has pleaded not guilty to all charges against him, and the allegations will continue to be examined as the case moves through the legal process.Speaking outside the courthouse after Tuesday's hearing, Patrick Steinfeld shared what he saw inside the courtroom. According to him, the photos shown as evidence were "gruesome" and difficult to look at.Steinfeld said the pictures were so upsetting that Celeste Rivas' mother, Mercedes Martinez, cried during the entire hearing and never recovered from seeing the images.He also described one moment when Deputy District Attorney Beth Silverman asked an LAPD detective what one of the photos showed. According to Steinfeld, the detective replied that it was Celeste's head. He claimed the condition of the remains was so severe that it was impossible to recognize them as a person's body.Steinfeld also said he believes the evidence presented during the hearing is He added that, in his opinion, D4vd should receive life in prison without the possibility of parole if he is found guilty.Prosecutors allege that D4vd lured Celeste Rivas to his Hollywood Hills rental home and killed her because they claim she was planning to expose their relationship. They further allege that her dismembered body was later left inside a Tesla registered to the singer.D4vd has denied all of the allegations. He has pleaded not guilty to every charge filed against him.The charges include first-degree murder with special circumstances. Prosecutors have also accused him of lying in wait, committing the crime for financial gain, murdering a witness to an investigation, lewd and lascivious sexual acts with a person under 14 years old, and mutilation of a human body.This is only the allegation of the prosecution, and there has been no verdict from any court as yet. The legal proceedings are still underway, and both sides will keep presenting their side as the case proceeds.This is where the preliminary hearing comes into play, as it gives the judge an opportunity to determine whether there is enough ground for the matter to proceed to trial. At the moment, D4vd continues to be considered innocent of all charges, as per the law, until he is convicted in a court of law.
Article Summary: Celeste Rivas' family lawyer says crime scene photos shown during D4vd hearing were 'gruesome' and difficult to look at. He said the images were so shocking that Celeste's mother cried throughout the hearing. He also described one moment when an LAPD detective told him that one of the photos showed the head of Celeste. The singer has pleaded not guilty to all charges against him.

Article Title: 'Toughest thing I do': Donald Trump honours four US soldiers killed in Middle East
Article Text:
Trump on Wednesday paid tribute to four American service members killed in the Middle East,

US President Donald Trump on Wednesday paid tribute to four American service members killed in the Middle East, attending a dignified transfer ceremony at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware as their remains were returned to the US.Trump saluted as four flag-draped transfer cases were carried from a military aircraft during the ceremony, which was also attended by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine, and members of Congress.Speaking later at an event in Georgia, Trump described the ceremony as "the toughest thing I do.""I've been there many times before. This was, in particular, something very sad," he said.Earlier in the day, Trump said his message to the grieving families was simple: "We love you. We love your child."The remains included two US Army soldiers killed in Iranian missile and drone attacks in Jordan, a third soldier believed to have died in the same attack after previously being listed as missing, and another soldier killed in Iraq in the detonation of an Iranian drone.The Pentagon identified the soldiers killed in Jordan as Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Hawaii, and Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Texas.The soldier believed to have been killed in the same attack was identified as Angel S. Rampersad, 28, of New York. The fourth service member, Michael Emmanuel Swinton, 30, of North Carolina, was killed in Iraq.Trump said Feehan's family travelled with him aboard Air Force One to Georgia. During his remarks, he remembered the young officer as "a flawless" person who "was going all the way — he was going to be a general."Addressing Feehan's parents, Trump said, "We will carry Tyler's memory in our hearts forever, and I just want to thank you. It's an honor to have you here today."Trump has repeatedly linked the deaths of the soldiers to the ongoing conflict with Iran."Those great people, those great patriots were out there fighting so that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon," he had said earlier this week, adding that US strikes on Iran were being carried out "in honor" of the fallen troops.On Monday, Trump also vowed retaliation for American casualties, saying, "Every time Iran kills an American soldier, they will pay for that killing many times over!"According to the administration, 18 US service members have been killed since the conflict began on February 28.Trump also said on Tuesday that while most incoming Iranian fire targeting US positions in Jordan had been intercepted, "They did slip something through in Jordan." He added, "If we had other operators, you know, it would have not happened, unfortunately... We let other people do the job — and sometimes it doesn't work out so well."The president did not elaborate on who he was referring to.The Pentagon said Feehan will be posthumously promoted to captain and awarded the Bronze Star, Purple Heart and Combat Action Badge. Gonzales, Rampersad and Swinton also served in air defence units, while Swinton will likewise receive the Bronze Star, Purple Heart and Combat Action Badge and be posthumously promoted to staff sergeant.
Article Summary: Trump saluted as four flag-draped transfer cases were carried from a military aircraft. The remains included two US Army soldiers killed in Iranian missile and drone attacks in Jordan. A third soldier believed to have died in the same attack after previously being listed as missing. Another soldier killed in Iraq in the detonation of an Iranian drone.

Article Title: Trump clears Saudi Arabia nuclear agreement, opens door to uranium enrichment
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump with Saudi crown Mohammed bin Salman (AP photo)

US President Donald Trump has approved a nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia that could allow the kingdom to develop uranium enrichment capabilities for its civilian nuclear programme, according to two people familiar with the decision.The sources quoted by Wall Street Journal, said it could be unveiled as early as Wednesday.The 30-year agreement is expected to involve US companies in developing Saudi Arabia's civilian nuclear programme. It could also pave the way for the construction of a uranium enrichment facility in the kingdom following a joint US-Saudi feasibility study.The agreement between the MAGA leader and the Islamic kingdom comes after months of heightened tensions between the United States and Iran, with much of President Donald Trump's fury focused on Tehran's nuclear ambitions.Both President Trump and former President Joe Biden sought to strike a civil nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia that would allow the kingdom to access US nuclear technology.However, non-proliferation experts have warned that permitting uranium enrichment inside Saudi Arabia could eventually give the kingdom the capability to pursue a nuclear weapons programme. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has previously indicated that Riyadh would seek nuclear weapons if Iran were to acquire an atomic bomb.Security concerns have also intensified in the region. Saudi Arabia and nuclear-armed Pakistan recently signed a mutual defence pact after Israel carried out strikes in Qatar targeting Hamas officials. Pakistan's defence minister later said Islamabad's nuclear programme "will be made available" to Saudi Arabia if required, a statement widely interpreted as a warning to Israel, which is widely believed to be the Middle East's only nuclear-armed state.While uranium enrichment alone does not enable a country to build a nuclear weapon, it must also develop several other complex technologies, including sophisticated explosives and weaponisation systems—it significantly lowers the technical barrier. That is why Western countries have long viewed Iran's enrichment programme with concern.In contrast, the United Arab Emirates signed a so-called "123 Agreement" with the United States to develop its Barakah nuclear power plant, built with South Korean assistance, without pursuing domestic uranium enrichment. Non-proliferation experts have often cited the UAE model as the "gold standard" for countries seeking civilian nuclear energy without raising proliferation risks.
Article Summary: The 30-year agreement is expected to involve US companies in developing Saudi Arabia's civilian nuclear programme. It could pave the way for the construction of a uranium enrichment facility in the kingdom following a joint US-Saudi feasibility study. Non-proliferation experts have warned that permitting uranium enrichment inside Saudi Arabia could eventually give the kingdom the capability to pursue a nuclear weapons programme.

Article Title: Tropical storm Bertha makes landfall in Louisiana, brings strong winds and flooding threat in US
Article Text:
NOAA satellite image taken at 11.40 am EDT on Wednesday shows the storm in the Gulf of Mexico moving toward the edge of Louisiana

Tropical Storm Bertha made landfall in southern Louisiana on Wednesday, bringing strong winds, storm surge and heavy rain to parts of the US Gulf Coast, while authorities warned residents to remain alert despite expectations that the system will steadily weaken.According to the National Hurricane Center , Bertha came ashore in St Bernard Parish, around 40 miles east of New Orleans, with maximum sustained winds of 45 mph (72 kmph). Tropical storm-force winds extended nearly 100 miles (160 km) from the storm's centre.The system prompted tropical storm warnings across parts of Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama, including New Orleans and Lake Pontchartrain. Beaches, parks, piers and some low-lying roads were closed as officials prepared for storm surge and flooding.Forecasters said coastal areas of Louisiana and Alabama could experience storm surges of up to 3 feet (1 metre), while rainfall of 1-4 inches (3-10 cm) is expected, with isolated locations likely to receive higher amounts.Louisiana state climatologist Jay Grymes said Bertha is likely to weaken quickly after moving inland and is not expected to cause widespread destruction. The impact on coastal communities should remain manageable, he said.Governor Jeff Landry described the outlook as "encouraging" but urged residents to stay prepared for possible flooding.The National Weather Service also noted an unusual overlap of tropical storm and extreme heat warnings across southern Louisiana, calling it a rare weather combination. It said this is the first such occurrence in the region in at least two decades, based on records dating back to 2005.Bertha is the second named tropical storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, following Tropical Storm Arthur, which brought heavy rainfall to the southeastern US in June. Forecasters warned Bertha could deliver more rain to parts of Mississippi that are still recovering from Arthur-related flooding.Elsewhere in the US, severe storms triggered tornado reports from Cincinnati to New Jersey, while flash floods in West Virginia inundated homes, damaged bridges and prompted multiple water rescues.In the eastern Pacific, Hurricane Fausto remained well offshore, hundreds of miles west-southwest of Baja California. The storm was packing maximum sustained winds of 80 mph (130 kmph) and is forecast to strengthen gradually. The National Hurricane Center warned that swells generated by Fausto could create dangerous surf and rip current conditions along the Baja California coast.
Article Summary: Tropical Storm Bertha made landfall in southern Louisiana on Wednesday. Authorities warned residents to remain alert despite expectations that the system will steadily weaken. Forecasters said coastal areas of Louisiana and Alabama could experience storm surges of up to 3 feet (1 metre)

Article Title: Mexican illegal immigrant working on California farm arrested over rape and assault charges
Article Text:
The man had previously been charged with rape and sodomy of a drugged victim.

An illegal immigrant working as an agricultural labourer in Southern California has been arrested after US border authorities said he had previously faced multiple serious criminal charges, including rape and sodomy of a drugged victim.US Customs and Border Protection's (CBP) El Centro Sector said its agents arrested the Mexican national while he was working in Thermal, a farming community in Riverside County, California. The agency did not identify the man but shared his photograph on social media.According to CBP, the man had previously been charged with rape and sodomy of a drugged victim, assault with a deadly weapon, and preventing or dissuading a witness or victim."Our agents from the Indio Station arrested an illegal alien from Mexico working as an agricultural worker in Thermal, CA," the agency said in a post on Instagram.Thermal, located about 25 miles southeast of Palm Springs in the Coachella Valley, is home to several agricultural operations, including farms producing dates and specialty crops.The arrest drew mixed reactions online, with some users praising the authorities and others commenting on the suspect's appearance.Immigration enforcement has remained a contentious issue in the Coachella Valley. Earlier this year, local lawmakers and immigrant rights advocates criticised federal enforcement operations in the region, arguing that they had disrupted families and businesses.Congressman Raul Ruiz had described the situation as a "public health crisis", saying parents had been detained, businesses had lost workers, and families were struggling to locate detained relatives.The arrest comes days after another immigration-related case involving an Indian national. An Indian national, Deepak Kumar, 31, of Fresno, California, is in the custody of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after Pennsylvania authorities accused him of transporting nearly $3 million worth of stolen tungsten oxide powder.According to The New York Post, investigators tracked a truck carrying 10 pallets of tungsten oxide powder, valued at about $2.86 million, after Mitsubishi Materials Corporation reported the shipment missing.Authorities said Kumar allegedly produced an invalid work visa, a fraudulent New York state driver's licence and a valid California driver's licence when stopped by police.He was arrested on theft-related charges before being transferred to ICE custody in California. Investigators said the industrial material is used in products such as armour-piercing ammunition, ceramics, lasers, optical equipment and specialised window coatings.
Article Summary: Mexican national arrested while working in Thermal, a farming community in Riverside County, California. He had previously been charged with rape and sodomy of a drugged victim, assault with a deadly weapon, and preventing or dissuading a witness or victim.

Article Title: Ousted Venezuelan president Maduro to face US drug trafficking trial in June 2027
Article Text:
File photo: Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro's initial appearance to face US federal charges (Picture credit: Reuters)

Defence to challenge indictment and legality of capture

US alleges cocaine trafficking conspiracy

Case unfolds amid changing US-Venezuela ties

Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, will go on trial in the United States on June 1, 2027, over drug trafficking charges after a federal judge approved the schedule on Wednesday.Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, have pleaded not guilty to charges that they conspired to traffic cocaine into the United States.If convicted, they could face life imprisonment. The couple has been held at a jail in Brooklyn since US forces captured them during a military raid in Caracas in early January and brought them to New York.US district judge Alvin K Hellerstein set the June 1, 2027 trial date after a request from both the prosecution and defence. Under the schedule, Maduro's legal team will begin filing motions in September seeking dismissal of the indictment.During Wednesday's hearing, defence lawyer Barry Pollack said he would first challenge the case on the grounds of sovereign immunity, arguing that Maduro, as the head of a sovereign state, should be immune from prosecution.If successful, Pollack argued, Maduro would not have to continue litigating the case.Pollack has also indicated that the defence intends to challenge the legality of Maduro's capture, describing it as a "military abduction". Maduro has similarly called himself a "prisoner of war" and described the US operation as a kidnapping.Neither Maduro nor Flores spoke during the 15-minute hearing. They have also not sought release on bail, according to news agency AP.US prosecutors allege that Maduro used his position as Venezuela's leader to facilitate the shipment of thousands of tonnes of cocaine into the United States by working with Venezuelan law enforcement and drug traffickers.Maduro faces four felony counts, including narcoterrorism conspiracy and conspiracy to import cocaine.At his arraignment in January, Maduro denied the allegations, saying, "I am not guilty. I am a decent man, the constitutional president of my country."The Trump administration has defended the January 3 military raid as lawful.An advisory opinion issued by the US Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel before the operation concluded that President Donald Trump could order the mission unilaterally because it served an important national interest and did not amount to a war requiring congressional approval.Maduro led Venezuela from 2013 until his capture in January. After his removal, former Vice President Delcy Rodríguez assumed leadership and has since established closer ties with the Trump administration.The report added that Washington has eased sanctions on Venezuela's oil industry, allowing foreign companies to expand oil and gas projects in the country.Ahead of the trial, Judge Hellerstein has scheduled a hearing on November 17 to consider the defence's motions seeking dismissal of the case, while additional legal challenges may be filed in early 2027 after prosecutors disclose any classified evidence.
Article Summary: Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, will go on trial in the United States on June 1, 2027. The couple has been held at a jail in Brooklyn since US forces captured them during a military raid in Caracas in early January and brought them to New York. Maduro's legal team will begin filing motions in September seeking dismissal of the indictment.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Elon Musk: "Being an entrepreneur is like eating glass and staring into…" - brutally honest lesson on entrepreneurship, resilience and the hidden reality behind building a business
Article Text:
Elon Musk

Quote of the day by Elon Musk

"Being an entrepreneur is like eating glass and staring into the abyss of death"

Where did Musk actually said it

What the two images are actually describing

Why the visible part of success hides most of the story

Why resilience tends to matter more than confidence

Other famous quotes by Elon Musk

"Failure is an option here. If things are not failing, you are not innovating enough."

"When something is important enough, you do it even if the odds are not in your favour."

"Persistence is very important. You should not give up unless you are forced to give up."

"Great companies are built on great products."

What it means in today's world

Entrepreneurship is often described as exciting, glamorous and full of promise. Elon Musk described it very differently. "Being an entrepreneur is like eating glass and staring into the abyss of death," he said, letting out his trademark cackle right after. He was not joking around for effect. He said this only months after taking Tesla public, during one of the hardest stretches of his own career, so the words came from real, lived experience rather than a rehearsed soundbite. It is one of the most honest lines ever said about starting a company, precisely because it skips the usual encouragement and simply describes what the experience actually felt like, without trying to make any of it sound easier than it was.Musk said this on stage at the Founder Showcase event in 2010, shortly after Tesla had gone public, in his first public appearance since the IPO. In that same conversation, he described December 2008 as one of the worst periods of his life, a stretch that included a failed SpaceX rocket launch, Tesla's funding falling through, and his own public divorce all happening within the same brief window.Musk later broke the metaphor down more precisely in a separate interview with Khan Academy, explaining "staring into the abyss" as the constant background awareness that the overwhelming majority of startups fail, meaning a founder is repeatedly telling themselves that getting the next decision wrong could genuinely end the company."Eating glass" he described as having to work on whatever problem the company actually needs solved, not the problem you would rather be working on, for as long as that discomfort continues.The public only sees the finished product, the launch, the funding round, the headline. What rarely gets seen is the string of failed experiments and stalled ideas that came before it, which most founders, including highly successful ones, go through repeatedly on the way to anything that actually works.Confidence gets someone started. It rarely determines whether they keep going once the plan stops working the way it was supposed to. Every business runs into obstacles nobody predicted, and the founders who keep adapting through those obstacles tend to end up in a stronger position over time than the ones who simply started out more certain of themselves.Technology has made it easier than ever to launch something new, but the underlying experience Musk described has not really changed. Building something genuinely new still means uncertainty, repeated setbacks, and long stretches of working on exactly the problem you would rather avoid. His line strips the glamour away deliberately, on the theory that anyone actually starting a company deserves the honest version rather than the comfortable one.
Article Summary: Musk said this on stage at the Founder Showcase event in 2010, shortly after Tesla had gone public, in his first public appearance since the IPO. It is one of the most honest lines ever said about starting a company, precisely because it skips the usual encouragement and simply describes what the experience actually felt like.

Article Title: MIT AI researcher warns replacing Gen Z with automation could be a billion-dollar mistake
Article Text:
MIT researcher says companies are breaking the apprenticeship model





Why Gen Z may be a company's biggest AI advantage

Entry-level job opportunities are becoming harder to find

Young graduates are increasingly worried about AI replacing jobs

History suggests young workers can adapt to technological change

Some major companies are expanding graduate hiring

The long-term cost may outweigh the short-term savings

Companies racing to replace entry-level employees with artificial intelligence may be saving money in the short term, but they could be creating a much bigger problem for the future, according to an MIT research scientist. Andrew McAfee, who co-leads the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Initiative on the Digital Economy, has warned that automating away junior roles could disrupt the talent pipeline that businesses rely on to develop future managers, specialists and leaders. He argues that removing entry-level jobs also means losing young employees who are often the quickest to embrace AI, potentially slowing innovation rather than accelerating it as organisations increasingly invest in automation.McAfee believes entry-level jobs serve a purpose far beyond completing routine tasks. They are the foundation on which employees develop practical knowledge, industry expertise and professional judgement through hands-on experience and mentorship.Speaking to Harvard Business Review, McAfee said people typically learn difficult knowledge work by first assisting experienced colleagues with routine responsibilities. If companies automate these tasks too quickly, they risk eliminating the apprenticeship ladder that has traditionally produced skilled professionals and future business leaders.While some employers see AI as a reason to reduce graduate hiring, McAfee argues the opposite.He believes younger workers represent one of the strongest competitive advantages in the AI era because they are generally more willing to adopt and experiment with emerging technologies.A Deloitte survey published in November 2025 found that 76% of Gen Z respondents had used a standalone AI tool, the highest adoption rate among all generations. McAfee noted that older workers are often more established in their routines, whereas younger employees tend to embrace new technologies more readily. Reducing entry-level hiring, he said, could deprive organisations of their most enthusiastic AI users.McAfee's warning comes as graduates already face a more challenging employment market. According to Handshake's Class of 2026 Network Trends Report, entry-level job postings have fallen by 2% compared with a year earlier and remain 12% below pre-pandemic levels.Data from the New York Federal Reserve also shows that the unemployment rate for college graduates aged between 22 and 27 stands at 5.6%, highlighting the growing difficulties many young professionals face when entering the workforce.Concerns about automation are rising sharply among students preparing to enter the job market. A survey by Monster found that nearly nine in 10 members of the Class of 2026 worry that AI or automation could replace entry-level positions. This marks a significant increase from 64% in the previous year's survey.The anxiety has also been fuelled by comments from technology executives, including Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei, who previously suggested AI could eliminate up to half of entry-level white-collar jobs before later softening that prediction.Despite growing concerns, historical evidence indicates younger workers have often adjusted successfully to previous waves of technological disruption. An analysis by Goldman Sachs found that college-educated young workers generally experience smaller long-term earnings losses than older displaced workers after losing their jobs.The report also found that younger employees are more likely to change occupations, learn new skills and move into roles that complement emerging technologies rather than compete directly with them. According to Goldman Sachs, occupational mobility and continuous skill development have historically helped young workers adapt to changing labour markets.Not every business is reducing entry-level recruitment. Several technology companies are instead investing more heavily in early-career talent as they expand their AI capabilities.IBM chief executive Arvind Krishna has said the company expects to triple its entry-level hiring and recruit more graduates than in recent years. Salesforce chief executive Marc Benioff announced plans to hire 1,000 graduates and interns to help develop the company's AI technologies. Amazon is also maintaining its graduate talent pipeline, with reports indicating it plans to hire around 11,000 software engineering interns in 2026, while AWS chief executive Matt Garman said demand for software developers continues to grow.McAfee's warning reflects a broader debate over how businesses should integrate artificial intelligence into their workforces. While AI can automate repetitive tasks and improve efficiency, he argues that removing entry-level opportunities could weaken companies' ability to develop future talent, adopt new technologies effectively and remain competitive in the years ahead.
Article Summary: MIT researcher says companies are breaking the apprenticeship model. Andrew McAfee believes entry-level jobs serve a purpose far beyond completing routine tasks. They are the foundation on which employees develop practical knowledge, industry expertise and professional judgement through hands-on experience and mentorship. McAfee's warning comes as graduates already face a more challenging employment market.

Article Title: A backyard chicken owner thought hens were eating the missing eggs, but later found five chicken snakes curled up inside the nest boxes
Article Text:
Backyard chicken owner blames hens for missing eggs, then finds 5 chicken snakes in nest boxes

Photo Credit: Reddit

Why coops attract snakes

Long-term solutions for backyard keepers

Gather eggs early: Collecting eggs multiple times a day, particularly early in the morning, removes the main reward for visiting snakes.

Collecting eggs multiple times a day, particularly early in the morning, removes the main reward for visiting snakes. Secure feed: Storing chicken feed in airtight containers and sweeping up spilled grain discourages mice and rats, eliminating the primary prey that attracts snakes in the first place.

Storing chicken feed in airtight containers and sweeping up spilled grain discourages mice and rats, eliminating the primary prey that attracts snakes in the first place. Block openings: Inspecting coops for gaps and sealing walls or floors with small-gauge hardware cloth prevents entry.

Inspecting coops for gaps and sealing walls or floors with small-gauge hardware cloth prevents entry. Adjust placement: Raising nest boxes off the ground and clearing heavy brush or debris around the perimeter removes hiding spots.

Understanding the 'chicken snake'

A backyard chicken owner who spent days suspecting their hens were eating their own missing eggs discovered the true culprits curled up in the coop: at least five chicken snakes nestled inside the nesting boxes.The flock owner shared the discovery online after empty nest boxes left them searching for answers. The incident is a proof of a common challenge faced by backyard poultry keepers, where warm coops, stored feed, and easy food sources regularly draw in wild reptiles."I hadn't been getting eggs for several days, I thought my chickens were eating them," the backyard chicken owner wrote on Reddit. "I went outside to check one day and I saw 5 or more chicken snakes in my nest boxes."Chemical deterrents provided only temporary relief for the poultry keeper."We bought some snake repellent powder and it worked for a couple weeks, but here over the last few days I have not seen any eggs again! How do I get rid of these snakes?" they asked the community.Fellow chicken owners offered a range of practical home remedies and structural fixes. One Redditor said, "We had a friend suggest the vanilla scented tree air fresheners.We hung a couple in the coop and so far so good." Others suggested safely trapping and relocating the reptiles, getting a barn cat or dog to ward them off, or advised to "put nest boxes higher up."Sheltered nest boxes filled with fresh eggs create an ideal feeding station for local wildlife. Human activities, such as building coops, storing grain, and providing covered nesting spaces, unintentionally attract both rodents and the snakes that hunt them.While missing eggs represent a financial loss for households relying on backyard flocks to offset grocery bills, wildlife experts note that snakes play a vital role in local ecosystems. They keep rodent populations under control, preventing pest damage to property and reducing disease transmission.Because repellents rarely work long term once reptiles locate a steady food supply, experts recommend humane prevention methods over chemical treatments.Effective coop defence focuses on removing access and food incentives:For persistent infestations or large numbers of reptiles, property owners are advised to consult local wildlife agencies or licensed humane removal specialists to manage the situation safely.The term "chicken snake" is actually a common nickname for rat snakes, a family of large, non-venomous reptiles native to many parts of North America. Because they are excellent climbers with flexible jaws, they often scale coop walls to hunt for wild bird eggs, small chicks, and mice. While seeing a five-foot snake inside a nesting box can be alarming, these reptiles possess no dangerous venom and are generally timid around humans, preferring to freeze or slither away when spotted.Rather than harming these animals, wildlife specialists suggest viewing rat snakes as helpful, natural pest controllers. They consume large amounts of rodents that would otherwise chew farm wiring, steal animal feed, and spread diseases. By making simple coop upgrades, like placing sturdy metal mesh over gaps and storing feed in sealed metal bins, chicken owners can protect their eggs while allowing harmless snakes to hunt pests elsewhere on the farm.
Article Summary: Backyard chicken owner blames hens for missing eggs, then finds 5 chicken snakes in nest boxes. The incident is a proof of a common challenge faced by backyard poultry keepers. Warm coops, stored feed, and easy food sources regularly draw in wild reptiles.

Article Title: From oil to atoms: Donald Trump to open nuclear door to Saudis
Article Text:
File photo: US President Donald Trump with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (Picture credit: Reuters)

TOI correspondant from Washington:

The Trump White House is expected to unveil a landmark 30-year civilian nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia on Wednesday in a deal that may reverberate far beyond the middle east while triggering a fierce debate in Washington over nuclear proliferation, regional security, and America's long-term interests.The proposed agreement, similar to the one with India under Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, would permit extensive US-Saudi civilian nuclear cooperation and eventually allow Riyadh to enrich uranium on its own soil under jointly agreed conditions. U.S firms led by Westinghouse are expected to play a central role in building Saudi nuclear infrastructure, a project potentially worth tens of billions of dollars.Unlike the "gold standard" agreement signed with the United Arab Emirates in 2009, Riyadh is not required to immediately renounce uranium enrichment or plutonium reprocessing, and the reported agreement also omits the International Atomic Energy Agency's Additional Protocol requiring more intrusive inspections. Those departures have alarmed non-proliferation experts and many lawmakers.Secretary of state Marco Rubio sought to reassure critics before the formal announcement, saying, "The US is not going to reach any agreement with any country in the world that leads to the risk of proliferation," while punting details of the deal to the White House.The administration broadly argues that bringing Saudi Arabia's nuclear ambitions under an American umbrella is preferable to allowing Riyadh to turn to China or Russia for nuclear technology, not to speak of sidelining Pakistan, which has long provided implicit nuclear cover for the Saudis. It also maintains the agreement would create thousands of American jobs while restoring a relationship strained by disagreements over the recent conflict with Iran and Saudi concerns about US regional commitments.Republican and Democrat lawmakers are expected to scrutinize the agreement when it reaches Congress, particularly because it appears to weaken safeguards that administrations had insisted upon. Congress can reject the agreement only by assembling a veto-proof majority, making outright defeat difficult, but there definitely be hearings that are bound to be contentious.The strongest concerns center on Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's repeated assertion that Saudi Arabia would acquire nuclear weapons if Iran developed one. That statement has become the principal argument for opponents who fear the agreement could accelerate a regional nuclear competition.Darya Dolzikova, Senior Research Fellow for Proliferation and Nuclear Policy at the Royal United Services Institute, argues that a US-Saudi accord has strategic merit because it can "help preclude a bigger Russian and/or Chinese presence in the region" and support America's nuclear industry. But, she cautions, "robust non-proliferation controls are paramount," particularly if enrichment remains an option.The timing of the deal, coming in the midst of the U.S-Iran war, is especially delicate. Washington has maintained that Iran should have "zero enrichment" capability while simultaneously considering a framework that could eventually permit Saudi enrichment, an apparent double standard that critics say risks undermining America's non-proliferation credibility.Meanwhile, the agreement presents an uncomfortable dilemma for Israel, which has traditionally opposed any regional enrichment capability outside its own undeclared nuclear deterrent, and which fears Saudi technological advances could eventually alter the regional balance, regardless of current political ties.Pakistan also figures prominently in the strategic calculus. For decades, Western intelligence assessments have suggested that Riyadh's close financial and military relationship with Islamabad could provide Saudi Arabia with an implicit nuclear hedge, although neither government has acknowledged such an arrangement publicly. By embedding Saudi Arabia's civilian nuclear program within an American framework, Washington may hope to reduce incentives for Riyadh to depend on Pakistan for strategic insurance while simultaneously deepening US influence over the kingdom's long-term nuclear trajectory.The agreement also carries implications for India, which has steadily expanded strategic partnerships with both Washington and Riyadh while strengthening energy, investment and defense ties with Saudi Arabia. A closer US-Saudi alignment could reinforce stability in Gulf energy supplies that are vital to India's economy. At the same time, any erosion of non-proliferation norms or a future regional nuclear competition would complicate India's security environment, particularly if Pakistan sought to leverage its historic strategic relationship with Saudi Arabia.Iran is almost certain to portray the agreement as evidence of American double standards after years of pressure on Tehran's enrichment program. Egypt and Iraq are likely to watch cautiously, wary of any shift in the regional strategic balance, while the UAE, which accepted far stricter restrictions under its own agreement, may privately question why Riyadh is receiving more permissive terms.Beyond the Middle East, the agreement represents a broader geopolitical contest. By anchoring Saudi Arabia's nuclear future to American technology and financing, the Trump administration is seeking to outmaneuver Beijing and Moscow in one of the world's most strategically important regions while reaffirming Washington's role as Riyadh's principal security partner. Whether that strategic gain outweighs the long-term proliferation risks will dominate the debate on Capitol Hill long after Wednesday's announcement.
Article Summary: U.S firms led by Westinghouse are expected to play a central role in building Saudi nuclear infrastructure. The administration argues that bringing Saudi Arabia's nuclear ambitions under an American umbrella is preferable to allowing Riyadh to turn to China or Russia for nuclear technology. The agreement presents an uncomfortable dilemma for Israel, which has traditionally opposed any regional enrichment capability.

Article Title: Borrowed ancestors: Why Pakistan can't claim Panini for its rebranding project
Article Text:
Indus Valley Civilization - Archaeological site of Harappa (Image Credit: Wikimedia Commons)

"Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it."

Ruins are not the same as inheritance

Heritage as reputation management

A civilisation is not a rebrand

— George SantayanaThe land now called Pakistan holds some of the subcontinent's oldest inheritances — the university-town of Takshashila, the brick avenues of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, the birthplace of the grammarian Panini, even a small bronze figure whose cocked hip and bangled arm art historians read as the earliest evidence of dance in South Asia, a gesture some trace forward into the classical grammar later refined into Kathak. For most of its seventy-eight years, the Pakistani state wanted remarkably little to do with any of it.This was not neglect. It was policy. The Two-Nation Theory did not simply carve out a homeland; it required a new ancestry to go with it. Pakistan's intellectual lineage was traced towards Arabia, Persia and Central Asia, and the Vedic, Sanskritic and Indus past lying beneath its own soil was filed away as someone else's prehistory — interesting to archaeologists, irrelevant to the nation. Mohenjo-daro was a curiosity. Takshashila was a footnote. The Dancing Girl was a museum exhibit, not an ancestor.That posture is changing, and the change is official. The Punjab government is currently running a heritage development plan worth close to four billion rupees to restore and rebrand Taxila as a premier tourist destination. Provincial budgets tout the restoration of Harappa and Rohtas Fort alongside Gandhara-circuit tourism drives.Mohenjo-daro is marketed abroad as a UNESCO showpiece. Panini, once an obscure name from a rejected past, is now claimed as a native son. History, apparently, is good for footfall.Consider that Dancing Girl a little longer. She was cast in bronze in Mohenjo-daro, in what is today Sindh, nearly four and a half thousand years ago. A second, cruder casting of the same figure was found beside her. When the subcontinent was partitioned, the finer of the two statuettes went to the National Museum in New Delhi, where she remains the single most reproduced image of the Indus Valley Civilisation. The lesser copy stayed behind, in Karachi. Pakistan inherited the ground she was found on. It did not inherit her.The same split runs through everything else Pakistan is now restoring for tourists. It can excavate a stupa at Taxila, but the unbroken line of Buddhist and Vedic scholarship that once animated that university has no living school inside its borders. It can point to the ruins of Harappa, but Sanskrit is not taught there in gurukulas the way it still is across India. It can rope off Mohenjo-daro for visitors, but the dance grammar its Dancing Girl is said to anticipate is taught today in the gharanas of Jaipur, Lucknow and Varanasi — not in Sindh or Punjab. Geography gave Pakistan the sites. It did not give it the tradition.Why the sudden enthusiasm, then? It is worth asking what else has been happening to Pakistan's standing in the world these past years — the terror-financing scrutiny, the repeated economic bailouts, the image of a state better known for instability than for scholarship. Ancient civilisation is good cover for a troubled present. A country associated with extremism can present itself instead as the cradle of the world's earliest cities and its most rigorous grammarian. Restoring Takshashila photographs well. It is also, transparently, a rebrand.There would be nothing wrong with genuine custodianship. But custodianship is judged by continuity, not by construction budgets. A state that spends on restoring temples and stupas as tourist infrastructure, while showing far less urgency about the living minority communities who are the actual cultural descendants of that civilisation within its own borders, is not practising heritage. It is practising public relations. Ruins do not complain about neglect. Living communities do.None of this is unique to Pakistan — every young nation wants an old civilisation behind it, for the same reason every parvenu wants an ancestral portrait on the wall. But there is a difference between a nation growing into an honest relationship with the past beneath its soil and a nation reaching for that past only once the present has become an embarrassment. The first is scholarship. The second is theatre.Panini's grammar, the ruins of Takshashila, the streets of Mohenjo-daro and the Dancing Girl who stands, unclaimed, in a Delhi museum are not props to be dusted off for a tourism campaign. They belong to a civilisational continuum that long predates Pakistan and that Pakistan's own founding ideology spent decades trying to disown. You cannot renounce an inheritance for seventy years and then present the paperwork the moment the neighbours stop calling.The Panini question, therefore, is not ultimately about Pakistan. It is about how civilizations endure. Nation-states are political arrangements. They emerge, fragment, redraw borders and sometimes disappear altogether. Civilizations operate according to a different logic. They survive because institutions, languages, rituals, philosophies and systems of knowledge are transmitted across generations with remarkable continuity. That continuity cannot be manufactured retrospectively simply because the archaeological site now falls within a different frontier.Panini illustrates this distinction with unusual clarity. His genius did not arise in isolation, any more than Newton's emerged without the European scientific tradition or Confucius without the intellectual world of ancient China. The Ashtadhyayi was the culmination of centuries of Vedic linguistic inquiry, drawing upon earlier traditions of phonetics, etymology and grammatical analysis. It belonged to an ecosystem of scholars, teachers and students extending across the cultural geography of ancient Bharat. His birthplace may today lie inside Pakistan's borders; the intellectual universe that produced him does not.That distinction also explains why heritage cannot be reduced to possession. A ruined monastery may be restored with public funds. A museum may renovate its galleries. Tourism campaigns may attract visitors. Yet the deeper life of a civilization lies not in stone but in continuity. Sanskrit is still spoken, taught and debated. The grammatical tradition Panini codified continues to be studied in universities, monasteries and traditional centres of learning. Classical dance, whose earliest artistic echoes some scholars discern in the Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro, survives through living lineages rather than archaeological exhibits. Civilizations remain alive because their knowledge systems remain alive.There is, in principle, nothing objectionable about Pakistan preserving Panini's birthplace or restoring the monuments of Takshashila and Harappa. Indeed, such efforts should be welcomed. The preservation of humanity's shared heritage is a universal responsibility. The problem begins only when conservation is quietly transformed into ownership, and ownership into civilizational authorship. Geography can preserve monuments; it cannot rewrite the intellectual traditions that created them.Perhaps this explains the growing attraction of ancient heritage within Pakistan's official narrative. Soft power increasingly matters in international politics. Nations seek legitimacy not only through military strength or economic performance but through cultural depth. Ancient civilizations offer prestige, tourism, diplomatic capital and a more attractive international image than perpetual association with conflict or extremism. The impulse is understandable. But prestige cannot rest upon selective memory. One cannot celebrate Panini while remaining intellectually detached from the Vedic and Sanskritic tradition that made Panini possible.History is often generous to those willing to confront it honestly. It is far less forgiving to those who edit it for contemporary convenience. Pakistan is free to acknowledge that some of the world's greatest centres of ancient learning stood on the land it now governs. What it cannot plausibly claim is that the civilization which produced them somehow begins where the modern Pakistani state begins. Civilizations are not inherited through borders. They are inherited through continuity. And continuity cannot be declared by policy, funded through tourism budgets or recovered by rebranding. It has to be lived.
Article Summary: The Punjab government is currently running a heritage development plan worth close to four billion rupees to restore and rebrand Taxila as a premier tourist destination. Restoring Takshashila photographs well. It is also, transparently, a rebrand. Pakistan inherited the ground she was found on. It did not inherit her.

Article Title: Govt school bombed in northwest Pakistan; no casualties reported
Article Text:
Representative image

PESHAWAR: Unknown militants blew up a government school in Pakistan's restive Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, officials said on Tuesday.No casualties were reported in the incident which took place late on Monday, and no group has claimed responsibility for it yet.According to initial reports, unidentified militants planted explosive material at Government Middle School Loi Kharki in the Bajaur district, causing a powerful explosion that extensively damaged the school building.Soon after the incident, law enforcement agencies and other relevant authorities reached the site and launched an investigation.Officials said efforts were underway to determine the nature of the explosion, identify those responsible and ascertain the motive behind the attack.Further investigation is in progress, officials added.According to investigative briefs from Human Rights Watch and the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, militants target educational structures for specific operational reasons.A vast majority of the targeted attacks directly hit girls' institutions to enforce extremist ideological bans against female literacy.

No casualties were reported in the incident which took place late on Monday, and no group has claimed responsibility for it yet. Law enforcement agencies and other relevant authorities reached the site and launched an investigation.

A recent surge in the alleged enforced disappearances of students and young people in Pakistan's Balochistan province has raised fresh concerns over the treatment of those linked to peaceful political organisations. Human rights activist Sammi Deen Baloch expressed her condemnation of the events and alleged that individuals are being taken from their homes, hostels and educational institutions.In a statement posted on X, Baloch described the development as alarming and a part of a broader pattern of enforced disappearances that has persisted in the restive province."The cycle of enforced disappearances in Balochistan has never truly stopped, but over the past few days in particular, there has been an alarmingly dangerous surge in the enforced disappearances of students," she said in a statement posted on X.The activist alleged that the disappearances were being justified as part of counter-insurgency operations, but argued that the approach had failed to bring peace to the restive province. Instead, she said, decades of such policies had deepened resentment and contributed to a cycle of unrest and violence."Abducting unarmed and innocent students, as well as young people affiliated with peaceful political organizations, from their homes, hostels, and educational institutions and forcibly making them disappear, and then justifying this oppression in the name of counter-insurgency, is a failed and inhumane state policy that has been imposed on Balochistan for decades," Baloch said, "If this approach were truly a means to bring peace, Balochistan would not be drowning today in this quagmire of blood, unrest, and hatred; rather, the reality is that this policy is not fostering peace but giving birth to even more hatred and violence.Baloch further alleged that young people were being held for years without being charged or brought before a court, and subjected to torture, humiliation and other forms of mistreatment. She argued that such treatment could itself fuel anger and a desire for revenge among those affected."When young people are held for years in state torture chambers without any crime or judicial process, subjected to inhuman violence, humiliation, and torment, it is the state itself that nurtures feelings of revenge and hatred against it through its own policies," she said.According to Baloch, when some of those who later reappear eventually turn to armed violence, state propaganda campaigns focus on those who speak out against enforced disappearances rather than examining the circumstances that may have contributed to the radicalisation of young people.She accused authorities of attempting to make the issue of enforced disappearances controversial by blaming peaceful political activists and human rights defenders for allegedly inciting people or recruiting them for armed groups.Baloch argued that the underlying causes of the continuing conflict were instead "illegal actions, state repression, and tyrannical policies", which she said continued to fuel hostility towards the state.She urged the authorities to review what she described as failed, unconstitutional and oppressive policies, and questioned why decades of alleged repression, enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings and collective punishment had failed to establish lasting peace in Balochistan."Instead of offloading the burden of its failed, unconstitutional, and oppressive policies onto the shoulders of the oppressed people and political and human rights activists, the state should ask itself why, despite decades of repression, enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings, and collective punishments, peace could not be established in Balochistan."The Pakistani government has previously rejected allegations of systematic enforced disappearances, maintaining that its security operations are conducted in accordance with the law and are aimed at combating militancy and maintaining public order.
