Article Title: HIV outbreak in Pakistan: How deadly safety lapses at Sindh hospital put children at risk
Article Text:
The SHCC's regulatory inspection found that used needles were not being disposed of in sharps bins, hospital staff could not explain disposal of needles (Photo credit: ANI)

At least 78 children have contracted HIV in an outbreak in Pakistan's Karachi linked to serious infection-control and medical waste management failures at a state-run hospital.Findings at the Sindh Employees Social Security Institution (SESSI)-run Valika Hospital in Karachi's SITE area revealed needles manually removed from syringes, inadequate sterilisation safeguards and untrained staff handling contaminated waste.The Sindh Healthcare Commission (SHCC), which conducted a regulatory inspection of the state-run hospital, found that used needles were not being disposed of in sharps bins. That hospital staff could not explain where the removed needles had gone or how they had been disposed of."This raised serious concerns about the hospital's medical waste management practices, as it was unclear where the removed needles had gone or how they had been disposed of," the healthcare commission said.The findings came after a major HIV outbreak at the hospital infected 78 children and led to the screening of more than 10,500 people living in the surrounding area.A further 120 people tested positive for HIV, while six deaths have been reported, according to Dawn.Independent inquiries into the outbreak found widespread failures in infection-prevention practices, including the dangerous reuse of single-use syringes. The findings have raised fresh questions over the safety of medical procedures and the handling of infectious waste at one of Sindh's state-run hospitals.During its inspection, the SHCC found that technical personnel were unable to tell inspectors how contaminated medical waste was being disposed of. The hospital had also failed to provide formal safety training to staff or produce written guidelines for handling medical waste and following infection-control procedures.The condition of the hospital's autoclave, a machine used to sterilise medical equipment, could not be verified. Nursing staff and operation theatre personnel were also absent from their posts during duty hours, making it difficult for inspectors to assess routine infection-control practices."The working condition of the autoclave could not be verified during the visit. Nursing and operation theatre (OT) staffs were also not available during duty time, which was making it difficult to assess routine infection control practices of their duty places," the regulatory body added.The SHCC also found that medical waste was not being segregated and disposed of according to infection prevention and control guidelines. Hospital staff had poor knowledge of safe medical waste handling, while the private contractor responsible for collecting and disposing of the waste had not received proper training."The team found that medical waste was not being segregated and disposed of according to IPC guidelines. Staff showed poor knowledge about safe medical waste handling. The private contractor responsible for collecting and disposing of medical waste had also not received proper training."The hospital's infection-control failures persisted despite the establishment of an Infection Prevention and Control Committee. The commission also cited staff unionisation and a lack of cooperation with safety protocols as factors that had compromised the handling of medical waste.Following independent inquiries, Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah ordered the suspension of 37 officers and officials, including administrators, laboratory personnel and nursing staff.The outbreak has renewed concerns over repeated failures in Pakistan's healthcare system. The country has faced several HIV outbreaks over the past decade, including the 2019 Ratodero outbreak, in which hundreds of children were infected. That investigation also exposed unsafe injection practices, poor sterilisation and weak oversight.The Sindh government has continued screening people in the affected area, promised treatment at public expense and announced a long-term fund for children affected by the outbreak. However, the Valika Hospital findings have raised concerns that similar infection-control failures could exist in other public and private healthcare facilities.
Article Summary: At least 78 children have contracted HIV in an outbreak in Pakistan's Karachi. The outbreak is linked to serious infection-control and medical waste management failures. Inspectors found needles manually removed from syringes, inadequate sterilisation safeguards and untrained staff handling contaminated waste.

Article Title: Pakistan's fifth province? Gilgit-Baltistan assembly passes key resolution amid PoK unrest
Article Text:
Gilgit-Baltistan (AP photo)

Is Pakistan preparing to make Gilgit-Baltistan its fifth province? Amid ongoing unrest in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, the Gilgit-Baltistan assembly has passed a resolution urging Islamabad to grant the region provisional provincial status, a move that could majorly redefine its administrative structure.The Gilgit-Baltistan assembly on Thursday passed a resolution, backed by both ruling and opposition sides, urging Islamabad to grant the region provisional provincial status, according to Dawn.The resolution, moved by lawmaker Jalal Ali Shah, also sought constitutional and political rights for the people of the mountainous region.Gilgit-Baltistan, located in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, currently has a semi-provincial administrative status.Pakistan currently has four provinces -- Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. If Islamabad accepts the proposal, Gilgit-Baltistan would become the country's fifth province under a provisional arrangement.
Article Summary: The Gilgit-Baltistan assembly has passed a resolution urging Islamabad to grant the region provisional provincial status. Pakistan currently has four provinces -- Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. If Islamabad accepts the proposal, Gilgit would become the country's fifth province under a provisional arrangement.

Article Title: 'Take off uniform and contest elections': Pakistani MP's open challenge to its military
Article Text:
Pakistani MP challenges their military ( Image quality improved using AI)

Critique on Baloch and Pashtun region

Critique of military

Petition filed against Fazl over remarks

Pakistani politician and chief of Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl, Maulana Fazlur Rehman, delivered a blistering critique of Pakistan's military and government, accusing them of failing to maintain order in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan while warning that the country's Pashtun regions were "drowning in blood.""The country is falling apart. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa today, there is no government. After the sun sets in the west, until the sun rises in the morning, the police do not step out of their stations. And if the police do not come out of their stations, then the streets will be handed over to armed groups, then the streets and roads will be at the mercy of bandits," Fazl said during a rally Punjab, Pakistan.He directly addressed the military: "I know your authority in my province — you have no government. You are just sitting inside your grand bungalows in the capitals, legs crossed, thinking you are the rulers. At the very least, in my province, you have no government."Fazl said Balochistan had already slipped out of government control and the Pashtun region was now following suit. "In Balochistan, in the Baloch areas, there were rebellions; the entire Baloch region had slipped out of Pakistan's control. Even today, there is no writ of the Pakistan government there.But we were holding back the Baloch region; now the Pashtun region too is drowning in blood."He described the human toll: "In the Pashtun region, within two or three days, we have received more than fifty bodies. All we did in the markets was buy shrouds for our loved ones. All we did was perform funerals for our loved ones."Fazl took aim at military personnel, accusing them of failing to protect citizens despite being paid from public taxes. "Your youth who are becoming martyrs — they have tied the uniform for this very reason, they are taking their salary for this very reason — that they have to fight for the country's security. What favor are you doing me by throwing your blood on me? You are taking your salary from the taxes of my blood and sweat for precisely this. "He added: "I have taken no salary; I will not form any army. You will leave, but you are pushing my homeland toward personal vendettas for generations to come, pushing it toward murder and plunder forever and ever. Explain this politics to someone else; don't try to explain it to us."Fazl challenged the military to enter politics directly. "If you want to do politics, then take off the uniform and come; participate in the elections, and it will become clear what votes people give to those in uniform. It is your prerogative to give government to whomever you want, and to snatch it away from whomever you wish."A petition was filed in a court against Fazl over his remarks, with the petitioner arguing that the speech hurt the sentiments of the general public and caused distress to the families of martyrs. The court sought a reply from the National Counter Terrorism Authority by August 17.Pakistani defence minister Khawaja Asif expressed disappointment, calling Fazl's words "unfair." Pakistan’s planning minister Ahsan Iqbal posted on X: "To describe such an unparalleled sacrifice as merely a compensation for a salary is neither fair, nor in accordance with the demands of ethics, and nor aligned with Islamic teachings."
Article Summary: Pakistani politician Maulana Fazlur Rehman delivered a blistering critique of Pakistan's military and government. He accused them of failing to maintain order in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. He warned that the country's Pashtun regions were "drowning in blood"

Article Title: 'Extreme brutality': Pakistan's PTI to launch nationwide protests for Imran Khan's release
Article Text:
.

The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf parliamentary party has decided to launch a nationwide movement from August 5 for the release of party chief Imran Khan and acceptance of other demands, a day that will mark the completion of the former prime minister's third year in prison.The decision was made at a meeting chaired by party's interim chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan at Khyber Pakhtunkhwa House in Islamabad, where PTI lawmakers discussed parliamentary affairs and the party's strategy going forward.PTI General Secretary Salman Akram Raja told Dawn that the movement would include public meetings, demonstrations and a long march. "It was also decided that Mehmood Khan Achakzai and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas's opinions will be sought for finalising the protest plans and other activities," he said.At a press conference, Gohar said the meeting discussed the health of Imran Khan and his spouse Bushra Bibi. He said August 5 would mark the completion of three years of the PTI founder's imprisonment and rallies would be held across the country to mark the occasion.Khan was arrested on August 5, 2023 after an Islamabad trial court found him guilty of corrupt practices in the Tosha Khana case. He has since been convicted in several cases and remains in solitary confinement at Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.Raja alleged that Khan had been kept in solitary confinement for months and that no one from his family or lawyers had been allowed to meet him since December last year. "He is not given proper medical care nor is he getting justice from the courts. The oppression and injustice in the country must come to an end," he said.He also warned the government not to launch a crackdown against party workers."Extreme brutality is being carried out here. Imran Khan is being denied meetings with his lawyers, while his sisters are also being barred from seeing him," Raja said as he sat surrounded by party workers outside the jail.Every week, Khan's sisters, lawyers and party workers gather outside Adiala Jail to press the government to allow the family to meet him. On June 14, Khan was taken to a hospital in Islamabad for treatment of his ailing right eye and later shifted back to prison.In a separate development, PTI lawyer Awais Younas Chaudhry submitted a list of six leaders to the Adiala jail administration for a meeting with Imran Khan. The list includes Haji Amanullah Awan, Muhammad Shahid Ali Chahan, Syed Hamid Ihsan, Sajjad Ali Butt, Noman Mughal and Aqsa Hayyat Lali.
Article Summary: The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf parliamentary party has decided to launch a nationwide movement from August 5. The decision was made at a meeting chaired by party's interim chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan. Khan was arrested on August 5, 2023 after an Islamabad trial court found him guilty of corrupt practices. He has since been convicted in several cases and remains in solitary confinement at Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.

Article Title: 'Protection of children is state's responsibility': Pakistan lawmaker seeks social media ban for under-16s
Article Text:
Representative image (AI-generated)

(With PTI inputs)

A lawmaker in Pakistan's Punjab has sought a ban on social media accounts for children under the age of 16 and also called for a similar action across the country.Sarah Ahmad of the Istehkam-e-Pakistan Party (IPP), a partner in the ruling coalition, moved the resolution in the Punjab assembly on Tuesday, marking the first such proposal in any provincial or federal legislature in Pakistan."The protection of children's physical, mental, psychological and moral development is both a constitutional and moral responsibility of the state. Unrestricted access to social media has exposed minors to cyberbullying, online sexual exploitation, inappropriate content, psychological distress, digital addiction and other serious online threats," the resolution said.It urged the federal government to enact legislation "prohibiting children below the age of 16 from creating or maintaining social media accounts unless parental or legal guardian consent is obtained through a reliable age-verification mechanism."The resolution also called on the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) to enforce effective age-verification systems across social media platforms operating in the country to ensure compliance with the proposed restrictions.The proposal comes amid growing global efforts to regulate children's use of social media, driven by mounting evidence linking excessive online activity to mental health issues, cyberbullying and exposure to harmful content.Several countries, including Australia and the UK, have introduced age-based restrictions or stronger child online safety measures, while others are considering tougher age-verification requirements for social media platforms.
Article Summary: A lawmaker in Pakistan's Punjab has sought a ban on social media accounts for children under the age of 16. Sarah Ahmad of the Istehkam-e-Pakistan Party (IPP), a partner in the ruling coalition, moved the resolution in the Punjab assembly on Tuesday.

Article Title: Two brothers detained by Pakistani forces found dead in Balochistan; custodial death concerns raised
Article Text:
Imam and Muhammad Umar, two labourers from Mand, were found dead with gunshot wounds after they were allegedly detained by Pakistani security personne

Two brothers who were allegedly taken into custody by Pakistani security personnel were later found dead in Balochistan's Kech district, with their bodies bearing bullet injuries, raising concerns around custodial treatment.The victims, identified as Imam and Muhammad Umar, were residents of Shaban Bazaar in Mand and were reportedly employed as labourers in Jiwani's Kuntani area, according to The Balochistan Post, cited by ANI.The brothers were travelling back to Mand on a motorcycle when they stopped near Balicha Cross after their vehicle reportedly ran out of fuel. Witnesses cited by the publication alleged that security personnel detained the two from the spot.The family later received their bodies through local police. Residents said both men had sustained gunshot wounds.The brothers were laid to rest in their ancestral village of Soro in Mand after funeral prayers. The incident has sparked concern among local residents, who questioned the circumstances leading to their deaths.The report said that before the identities of the deceased became known, several pro-military social media accounts claimed that two suspected militants had been killed during a security operation in the area.However, residents disputed those claims, identifying the deceased as the two labourers and insisting they had no militant links.There has been no official response from Pakistan's military or government regarding the alleged detention or the deaths.Paank, the human rights wing of the Baloch National Movement (BNM), condemned the incident, alleging that the brothers were victims of an extrajudicial killing. The organisation urged authorities to order an independent and transparent investigation and called for accountability if the allegations are proven.
Article Summary: Imam and Muhammad Umar were labourers in Jiwani's Kuntani area. They were travelling back to Mand on a motorcycle when they stopped near Balicha Cross. Witnesses said security personnel detained the two from the spot. The family later received their bodies through local police. Both men had sustained gunshot wounds.

Article Title: LeT, IS operatives among 34 killed in Khuzdar attack: BLA
Article Text:
File photo

In a morale booster for its cadre, Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) has released a statement detailing its massive, coordinated suicide attack on the fortified compound of ISIS-K commander Shafiq Mengal in Pakistan's Khuzdar city last week, claiming to have killed 34 operatives, including terrorists from Lashkar-e-Taiba besides Islamic State In the statement, which stands out for its confident undertone, the rebel group claimed responsibility for the operation - which involved vehicle-borne explosives and a team of suicide bombers - framing it as the official commencement of a broader offensive named "Operation Murg-e-Ghadaran".The attack took place during a gathering at the compound that included Pakistani intelligence officials, operatives from international militant networks, including ISIS and LeT, and former Afghan soldiers, who were reportedly meeting to coordinate efforts against the Baloch political movement, the BLA revealed in its statement. This has yet again exposed the proximity between Pakistan's ISI and Islamic State factions that are being used to quell the Baloch freedom struggle.Falsely accusing India's hand in the incident, Mengal, who survived the attack, said that 17 of his associates, who were having a meal, were killed in an explosion. He said the attackers later engaged in an armed clash with those inside the compound. The assault was executed by BLA's specialised self-sacrificing wing Majeed Brigade.The operation was allegedly set in motion following weeks of strict surveillance by BLA's intelligence wing Zirab, which tracked a high-level meeting.BLA asserted that 34 people killed in the firefight were primary members of Mengal's private network, whom they accused of direct involvement in targeted killings, abductions and enforced disappearances of Baloch political activists and students.
Article Summary: Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) released a statement detailing its massive, coordinated suicide attack on the fortified compound of ISIS-K commander Shafiq Mengal. The attack took place during a gathering at the compound that included Pakistani intelligence officials, operatives from international militant networks, including ISIS and LeT.

Article Title: Healthcare crisis in Pakistan: Shortage of 100 life-saving medicines like cancer drugs, morphine
Article Text:
Healthcare crisis in Pakistan: Islamabad faces shortage of 100 life-saving medicines, including cancer drugs, morphine & vaccines (Representative ANI, IANS image)

Pakistan is facing a severe shortage of more than 100 essential medicines, including life-saving drugs used to treat cancer, heart disease and other serious illnesses, after delays in approving revised medicine prices disrupted production, according to a report by Dawn.The report said the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP) recommended revised prices for 105 medicines under the hardship category more than two years ago after concluding that rising production costs had made their manufacture commercially unviable. However, the proposals remain pending before the federal cabinet, leading to reduced production and widespread shortages.According to Dawn, DRAP found that higher prices of imported raw materials, electricity, fuel, packaging, transportation, labour, financing costs and the depreciation of the Pakistani rupee had sharply increased manufacturing expenses. Pharmaceutical companies have argued that the existing pricing policy no longer allows them to recover production costs, forcing several manufacturers to cut output or stop producing essential medicines.The shortages include oral morphine for cancer patients, streptokinase injections used to treat heart attacks, chemotherapy drugs such as cisplatin, carboplatin and doxorubicin, paediatric digoxin, pilocarpine eye drops and yellow fever vaccines, the report said.Abdul Samad Buddani of the Pakistan Chemists and Druggists Association warned that the continued shortage of genuine medicines was creating space for counterfeit and substandard products in the market.According to Dawn, Buddani said desperate patients were increasingly turning to unreliable sources, raising concerns over the safety and authenticity of medicines, particularly expensive cancer treatments and other critical drugs.Industry representatives have urged the government to immediately approve the pending hardship pricing cases, warning that further delays would worsen shortages and disrupt healthcare services. A senior representative of the Pakistan Pharmaceutical Manufacturers' Association said manufacturers could not continue producing essential medicines if they were unable to recover even basic production costs, Dawn reported.The medicine shortage comes amid mounting pressure on Pakistan's public healthcare system. Earlier this month, house officers at Karachi's Abbasi Shaheed Hospital intensified protests over unpaid stipends, inadequate security and a shortage of medicines, warning they would suspend outpatient department (OPD) services if their demands were not met, according to The Express Tribune.
Article Summary: Pakistan is facing a severe shortage of more than 100 essential medicines. The drugs include life-saving drugs used to treat cancer, heart disease and other serious illnesses. Delays in approving revised medicine prices have disrupted production. Pharmaceutical companies have argued that the existing pricing policy no longer allows them to recover production costs.

Article Title: Balen ends envoy snub amid protests, to meet India & China ambassadors
Article Text:
Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah. (AFP file photo)

NEW DELHI: Nepal prime minister Balendra Shah is set to break his self-imposed rule of avoiding one-on-one meetings with foreign diplomats by holding separate talks with Indian ambassador Naveen Srivastava and Chinese ambassador Zhang Maoming this week, a diplomatic reset that comes as his govt faces growing street protests and questions over its early policy choices. The two meetings are expected to be held on the same day, an arrangement meant to signal that both India and China remain central to Nepal’s foreign policy.Shah took office on March 27 after riding a Gen Z-driven political wave that promised a break from Nepal’s old political order, but his first weeks in power were marked by an unusual diplomatic posture. He avoided individual meetings with envoys and visiting officials who would ordinarily expect one-on-one access to Nepal’s head of govt, including India’s foreign secretary Vikram Misri, whose Kathmandu visit was postponed after Shah declined to meet him. It was the same story with senior US diplomats, including assistant secretary of state Samir Paul Kapur, who visited Kathmandu in April.Shah’s aides had framed the approach as a "new protocol" under which the PM would not hold one-on-one meetings with foreign officials below foreign minister level, leaving such engagements to foreign ministry channels or collective briefings. Shah also accepted PM Narendra Modi’s invitation to visit India soon after taking office, but that visit has still not taken place.Meanwhile, RSP chairman Rabi Lamichhane received a high-profile welcome in New Delhi in June.Lamichhane’s visit sharpened the contrast. He met Modi, home minister Amit Shah, external affairs minister S Jaishankar, NSA Ajit Doval, Misri and BJP president Nitin Nabin, among others, signalling that New Delhi had opened its top political, diplomatic and security channels to Nepal's ruling party chief.Shah did receive ambassadors and heads of diplomatic missions collectively on April 8. At that meeting, attended by representatives from 17 countries and the United Nations, he spoke of a “balanced and pragmatic foreign policy” and relations based on “trust, mutual respect and shared prosperity”. His govt later presented the format as part of stricter enforcement of Nepal’s "diplomatic code of conduct".Officials familiar with the new development said the decision to begin separate meetings with India and China was deliberate. “It is natural to begin with ambassadors of our two neighbours, India and China, given Nepal’s foreign policy priorities,” an official said, adding that scheduling the meetings on the same day was meant to avoid any perception of preference.The shift comes shortly after Shah’s govt completed 100 days in office, a period in which the street energy that helped bring him to power has begun turning towards his own administration. Protests have broken out over the use of municipal police and bulldozers against Kathmandu’s landless settlements, street vendors and informal workers, with critics saying the city’s poorest residents have borne the sharpest edge of his governance style.Border communities also protested strict enforcement of customs duty on goods worth more than Nepali Rs 100 brought from Indian markets. Anger deepened further after 25-year-old ride-hailing driver Ganesh Nepali set himself ablaze following municipal police action, bringing Gen Z activists, civil-rights voices, informal workers and displaced residents back to the streets.
Article Summary: Nepal's prime minister Balendra Shah is set to break his self-imposed rule of avoiding one-on-one meetings with foreign diplomats. He will hold separate talks with Indian ambassador Naveen Srivastava and Chinese ambassador Zhang Maoming this week.

Article Title: World's 'happiest' nation facing youth exodus crisis: Gelephu Mindfulness City is Bhutan's unique solution
Article Text:
Gelephu Mindfulness City, a high-tech, culturally anchored urban experiment. (Artist's impression)

The 'happiness' factor

Why the youth are leaving

What Bhutan's National Statistics Bureau data reveals

Why go-to fixes failed

Mindfulness City

All you need to know about Gelephu

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe Bhutan can successfully keep its youth from migrating abroad? Yes, with the right policies No, migration is inevitable 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Why the project matters for India

Bhutan PM Tshering Togbay on Gelephu

PM Modi on Gelephu

The big picture

Bhutan has long been the soft, poetic rebuke to a world defined by GDP figures and glitzy 'smart' development models.For decades it has marketed itself — and, more importantly, governed itself — around Gross National Happiness (GNH), a state philosophy that values well‑being, cultural preservation, environmental stewardship, and good governance over raw economic output.Yet beneath the postcard façade, Bhutan confronts a wrenching reality: its youth are leaving in unprecedented numbers.Despite its global branding as the "world’s happiest country", mounting demographic, economic, and social stresses are pushing the nation’s young people to look beyond its Himalayan borders. The country that measures success through happiness faces a paradox — how do you keep a generation content enough to stay when opportunities, mobility, and aspirations pull them outward?To battle the crisis, the country's policymakers and thinkers are rolling out an ambitious concept that is typically Bhutanese: Gelephu Mindfulness City, a high-tech, culturally anchored urban experiment intended to marry economic opportunity with ingrained spiritual and environmental values.This is how a nation built on contentment is trying to stop a brain drain by reinventing what “success” looks like.But before we take a look at the solution, let's decode the crisis facing Bhutan.Bhutan's GNH Index is a unique way the country measures its people's overall well-being instead of just economic growth. Unlike most nations that focus on GDP, Bhutan believes true progress includes mental, social, and environmental health.The GNH Index is built on nine key areas of life: psychological well-being, health, education, time use, cultural diversity, good governance, community vitality, ecological diversity, and living standards. Every few years, the government conducts nationwide surveys asking citizens about these aspects, such as their life satisfaction, sleep, work balance, family ties, and environmental values.People are grouped as deeply happy, extensively happy, narrowly happy, or unhappy, depending on how many indicators they fulfill.The GNH, however, is often misread as proof that the country is the "happiest on earth", but that headline masks a more complicated reality.While GNH reflects Bhutan's unique philosophy of prioritising well-being over GDP, it does not mean citizens are universally content or free from hardship.In global happiness rankings, such as the World Happiness Report, Bhutan typically places around the middle — not at the top.Bhutan’s population is small — about 800,000 — and even modest outflows can distort social and economic balance.Over the last decade youth unemployment, underemployment, and limited higher-education capacity have driven larger cohorts to India, Australia, and beyond for study and work.Bhutan's National Statistics Bureau show increasing temporary and permanent emigration among the age group of 18-35.Bhutanese youth, more connected and aspirational than earlier generations, seek modern career pathways — tech, creative industries, international finance — that the domestic economy struggles to supply.The migration's social costs are multifold.Families lose young wage-earners and future caregivers; rural communities see accelerated aging and labour shortages; the public sector faces recruitment challenges; and the political compact that has long underpinned Bhutan’s social model — citizens invested in a shared cultural and ecological future — comes under strain.External remittances can prop up household incomes short-term but do not build domestic industrial capacity or broaden opportunity inside Bhutan.More significantly, an exodus of young minds weakens cultural renewal — problematic for a nation that takes continuity of identity seriously.Policymakers tried textbook responses to the exodus crisis: expand technical and vocational training, incentivise entrepreneurship, liberalise small-business credit, and pursue FDIs in tourism and light manufacturing. These moves matter, but they collide with structural constraints — geography, a tiny domestic market, limited physical infrastructure, and a deliberate policy preference to limit mass urbanisation and environmental degradation.Bhutan’s constitutional and policy emphasis on preserving culture and environment restricts large-scale industrialisation, while its hydropower-centric growth model offers limited employment multipliers for the modern service and knowledge economy.A new approach needed three elements simultaneously: meaningful job creation aligned with global demand, preservation and modernisation of cultural values, and place-making that makes staying emotionally and socially attractive.Enter Mindfulness City, Bhutan's nascent urban vision. No skyscrapers, highways, massive transport infra and soul-crushing concrete mazes.At its core, Mindfulness City reframes “development” as an integrated proposition: economic opportunity, environmental stewardship, social cohesion, and mental wellbeing — so that modern aspirations are met without sacrificing the emotional and ecological frameworks that define Bhutanese identity.It is less a single project and more a networked policy portfolio: special economic zones for creative technology, campuses for experiential and Himalayan studies, climate-resilient housing anchored by communal public spaces designed for contemplative practice, and tightly controlled tourism nodes that pay locals well and preserve authenticity.Crucially, it anchors economic incentives to GNH-compatible metrics: projects will be evaluated by impact on community well-being, environmental health, and cultural continuity as much as by profit.This balanced approach is designed to answer a key question: can a small nation create a modern urban ecology that satisfies career ambition and cosmopolitan desire, while preserving the psychological and social benefits that defined its national identity?Mindfulness City is not purely hypothetical.Pilots in and around Thimphu and in planned satellite nodes show proof-of-concept: digital nomad visas tied to service provision, a climate data center employing local graduates, and a community-run eco-hospital that blends western medicine with traditional healing practices. Early hires include Bhutanese returnees with engineering and data-science backgrounds working on trans-Himalayan climate modeling—roles that didn’t exist a decade ago in Bhutan.These pilots have produced encouraging metrics: a decline in short-term out-migration from participating districts, higher local retention of graduates in those sectors, and nascent startup formation with Bhutanese founders. Yet the scale is small, and skepticism remains about whether these pilot wins can scale across diverse geographies and social strata.Bhutan’s choices don’t exist in a vacuum. The kingdom sits between India and China, with New Delhi being a dominant security and economic partner.For New Delhi, Bhutan is not just a friendly neighbour; it is a strategic buffer, a hydrological partner, and one of India’s closest and most trusted relationships in the Himalayas. That means any major Bhutanese development project, even one framed as cultural or urban renewal, inevitably carries geopolitical weight.For decades, India has been engaged in Bhutan's infrastructure and education linkages, often in a manner that preserves Thimpu's policy autonomy.This cooperation has extended to Bhutan's ambitious Mindfulness City, which is coming up on the border of Assam's Chirang district.Besides an international airport, the city will also be linked via railway with India.During his trip to Bhutan in November last year, PM Narendra Modi announced the decision to establish an Immigration Check Post at Assam's Hatisar to facilitate easy movement of investors and visitors to Gelephu.India and Bhutan also signed a Memorandum of Understanding on the establishment of two cross-border rail links — Kokrajhar (Assam)–Gelephu (Bhutan) and Banarhat (West Bengal)–Samtse (Bhutan) — to be built at a cost of ₹4,033 crore. The Kokrajhar–Gelephu line will span 69km, while Banarhat–Samtse will cover 20km.The project was virtually inaugurated by PM Modi on March 13 this year.Speaking at a programme in Thimphu marking the 70th birthday of Bhutan's fourth King Jigme Singye Wangchuck, PM Modi said the project would deepen economic and infrastructural cooperation between the two nations.“Along with energy cooperation, our focus is on enhancing connectivity between India and Bhutan because connectivity creates opportunity and opportunity creates prosperity,” he said, adding: "The progress and prosperity of India and Bhutan are closely linked."That is why Mindfulness City matters beyond architecture or branding.If it succeeds, it could slow youth migration, expand domestic opportunity, and reduce the pressure for Bhutanese professionals to seek futures elsewhere.For India, that is important because large-scale outmigration from Bhutan would not just weaken Bhutanese society; it could also increase the pull of India as a labour, education, and transit destination, while making Bhutan more vulnerable to external influence.A stronger Bhutan is easier for India to work with, and far less likely to become a geopolitical opening for China or other outside actors.Bhutan's youth exodus is a wake-up call for any culture that assumes spiritual values alone can anchor modern generations.But the country's challenge is not to stop youth from wanting more. That desire is natural, universal and often healthy.The real task is to make a compelling case that "more" need not mean "elsewhere".Mindfulness City is a plan to make staying an active choice, not a fallback. It is an attempt to prove that modern urban life and spiritual well‑being can coexist — not as a marketing ploy, but as lived reality. It's a philosophical test — can a society scale well-being as an organising principle for economic modernisation?If this works, Bhutan could take its global moral project — happiness measured against wellbeing — and show how to operationalise it where it matters most: in the daily decisions of its people. And the world will get a new template of development where the calculus of migration shifts from "where do I earn the most" to "where do I live my fullest life?".
Article Summary: Bhutan has long marketed itself as the 'world's happiest country' But mounting demographic, economic, and social stresses are pushing the nation’s young people to look beyond its Himalayan borders. How do you keep a generation content enough to stay when opportunities, mobility, and aspirations pull them outward? To battle the crisis, Bhutan is rolling out an ambitious concept that is typically Bhutanese: Gelephu Mindfulness City.

Article Title: Bangladesh to try retired army major under military law in ex-president Ziaur Rahman assassination case
Article Text:
Fugitive in Ziaur Rahman assassination case arrested by Bangladesh detectives

(With PTI inputs)

NEW DELHI: Bangladesh has handed over a retired army major to the military for trial under military law over his alleged role in the 1981 assassination of then-President Ziaur Rahman, father of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.Major (retd.) Mozaffar Hossain was arrested last week from the Defence Officers Housing Scheme (DOHS) in Dhaka's Banani area."Major (retd.) Mozaffar Hossain has been arrested and handed over to the Bangladesh Army for trial under military law," home minister Salahuddin Ahmed told reporters.According to Ahmed, the retired officer had been a fugitive for several years in a "neighbouring country," without identifying it."The major's other associates were tried by a military court at the time, and certain observations were recorded in those proceedings. He had remained a fugitive for many years in a neighbouring country under a different identity," the minister added.Explaining why Hossain would face trial under military law, Ahmed noted that this is because there is "no legal provision to try an individual separately under both civil and military laws for the same offence.""Therefore, the trial in this case will be conducted under military law," he stated.Rahman, a military ruler-turned-politician, was assassinated in the southeastern port city of Chattogram on May 30, 1981.Following a general court-martial in the case, 13 military officers were hanged, while five others received varying prison terms.According to official records, military and police investigations at the time identified Hossain as an "active or direct participant" in the coup that led to Rahman's assassination.Rahman's wife, Khaleda Zia, who died in December last year, was Bangladesh's first woman prime minister.
Article Summary: Major (retd.) Mozaffar Hossain was arrested last week from the Defence Officers Housing Scheme (DOHS) in Dhaka's Banani area. The retired officer had been a fugitive for several years in a "neighbouring country," without identifying it.

Article Title: Nepal's Re 1 coin gets a makeover: Controversial Kalapani-Lipulekh-Limpiyadhura map removed
Article Text:
Nepal's Re 1 coin gets a makeover: Controversial Kalapani-Lipulekh-Limpiyadhura map removed (Image/X)

Background of the dispute

The Nepal government has approved the minting of a newly designed one-rupee coin, replacing the country's controversial map that included the disputed areas of Limpiyadhura, Lipulekh and Kalapani with the image of an ancient monastery.The decision comes years after Nepal's then KP Sharma Oli-led government introduced a new political map in 2020 showing the three disputed territories as part of Nepal, triggering a diplomatic row with India. Nepal claims Lipulekh, Kalapani and Limpiyadhura as its territory, while India maintains that the areas belong to it.According to cabinet sources, Nepal's Council of Ministers approved the Nepal Rastra Bank's proposal on Thursday to mint redesigned one-rupee and two-rupee coins, PTI reported.As part of the redesign, the controversial political map will be removed from the one-rupee coin and replaced with the image of the Lo Ghyakar Monastery, located in Marang village in Mustang district. The monastery is regarded as one of Nepal's oldest Buddhist monasteries.However, the two-rupee coin will continue to carry the map introduced earlier, PTI reported citing cabinet sources.The proposal is part of a broader redesign by the Nepal Rastra Bank to reduce the size and weight of coins.Bank spokesperson Guru Prasad Paudel said the new one-rupee coin will weigh 3.2 grams instead of 4 grams, while the two-rupee coin will weigh 3.8 grams instead of 5 grams. Both coins will be made of steel instead of mixed metal and will have a steel-white colour instead of the current yellow finish.The decision has drawn criticism from senior Nepali Communist Party leader Bhim Rawal, who described it as a move against Nepal's territorial integrity."If the government led by Prime Minister Balen Shah has indeed decided to remove the map of Nepal, including Limpiyadhura, Lipulekh and Kalapani, from the one-rupee coin and replace it with the image of the Lo Ghyakar Monastery, it will constitute another serious anti-national decision and a blow to Nepal's territorial integrity," Rawal said.He also demanded that the government and the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party immediately clarify the decision.The controversy dates back to May 2020, when Nepal's then prime minister KP Sharma Oli unveiled a new official political map incorporating Lipulekh, Kalapani and Limpiyadhura as part of Nepal. The move came after India inaugurated a road connecting Dharchula in Uttarakhand to Lipulekh Pass, a key route for the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage.The three areas lie near the India-Nepal-China tri-junction and have long been disputed. Nepal argues that, under the 1816 Sugauli Treaty with British India, the Mahakali River forms the boundary between the two countries and that the disputed territories lie east of the river, making them part of Nepal. India maintains that the boundary follows a different origin of the river and considers the areas part of Uttarakhand.The dispute has strategic significance because Lipulekh Pass provides India with an important route to Kailash Mansarovar and serves as a key vantage point for monitoring Chinese military activity along the border. Since the 1962 India-China war, the Kalapani area has been manned by the Indo-Tibetan Border Police.
Article Summary: Nepal has approved minting of a newly designed one-rupee coin. Controversial Kalapani-Lipulekh-Limpiyadhura map removed from coin. New coin will carry image of Lo Ghyakar Monastery, one of Nepal's oldest Buddhist monasteries.

Article Title: Is all well in Balen Shah's Nepal? Why protests are testing his promise of change
Article Text:
Just over 100 days into office, Nepal's Prime Minister Balen Shah is facing growing protests from many of the same young supporters who helped bring him to power.

How Balen Shah came to power

Balen Shah's rapid ascent was fuelled by public anger at corruption and a demand for a new political order

A bumpy first hundred days

Bulldozers by the Bagmati, and a match that lit a fire

The silence behind the sunglasses

The Nepali Congress has repeatedly urged the government to engage with critics rather than dismiss them.

A govt still finding its footing

A little over 100 days into office, Nepal's youngest prime minister is already facing the kind of anger that swept his predecessor from power.When Balendra "Balen" Shah took office in March, he carried the hopes of a generation that had grown tired of corruption, political dynasties and empty promises.The rapper-turned-engineer-turned-politician was not just another elected leader; he was the face of a political reset born from the Gen Z uprising that shook Nepal in 2025.But revolutions have a habit of creating impossible expectations. Barely three months later, protesters are back on Kathmandu's streets.Last week, youth in Nepal gathered outside the deparment of passports in Tripureshwar. They were not there for paperwork. They were mourning a 25-year-old ride-share driver named Ganesh Nepali, who had set himself on fire days earlier after a dispute with traffic police over a fine he could not afford.That government is led by Balendra "Balen" Shah, a rapper-turned-engineer-turned-politician who became Nepal's youngest ever prime minister in March 2026.Barely a hundred days into office, his administration is now facing the same kind of street pressure that toppled his predecessor.Protesters took to roads over forced evictions of riverside squatters, over police conduct, and now over Ganesh Nepali's death. Some are demanding Shah's resignation outright.Shah rose to national power on the back of the 2025 Gen Z uprising, a youth-led revolt that burned down Nepal's parliament and forced a four-time prime minister out of office.Many of the same young people who cheered his landslide election victory in March are now among his loudest critics.Balen Shah's political story began long before he entered government. He trained as a structural engineer, but it was his career as an underground rapper that made him a household name among young Nepalis. His lyrics attacked corruption, broken infrastructure and social inequality, themes that resonated with a generation frustrated by the same old political families running the country.In 2022, Shah turned that popularity into votes and won the Kathmandu mayoral race as an independent candidate, the first person to do so. As mayor, he pushed through reforms in waste management and traffic control, and he took an aggressive approach to clearing pavements, street markets and informal squatter settlements. Those evictions drew criticism even then, but his energetic style made him a popular figure well beyond the capital.The turning point came in September 2025. A government ban on Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram, combined with long-simmering anger over corruption and nepotism among the political elite, sent thousands of young Nepalis onto the streets. Security forces responded with force, and over two days of unrest, dozens of protesters were killed and parliament was set ablaze. Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli resigned, and Nepal was placed under an interim government led by Sushila Karki Shah, still Kathmandu's mayor at the time, was swept up in the mood of the moment. In a since-deleted midnight social media post, he lashed out at almost every established political party and foreign power in the same breath. Months later, he resigned as mayor and joined the Rastriya Swatantra Party, a young anti-establishment party led by former broadcaster Rabi Lamichhane.When Nepal went to the polls in March 2026, the RSP won an extraordinary 182 of 275 seats, the largest single-party mandate since Nepali democracy was restored in 1991. Shah, then 35, was sworn in as prime minister on March 27. Within hours, his government had ordered the arrest of Oli and his former home minister over their role in the September deaths.The early weeks of Shah's government were meant to showcase a clean break from Nepal's old politics. Instead, they exposed how fragile that break could be. His first cabinet reshuffle came within a fortnight, when the labour minister was sacked for breaching party discipline. Then, less than a month into the job, Home Minister Sudan Gurung resigned amid a growing scandal over his personal finances.Gurung had founded the volunteer organisation Hami Nepal and had been one of the central organisers of the 2025 protests that brought Shah to power.His resignation followed reports linking him to a businessman under investigation for money laundering, and to shareholdings he had not declared. Days later, in an unusual move, President Ram Chandra Paudel suspended both houses of parliament altogether, a decision opposition leaders called unprecedented. Shah himself took charge of the Home Ministry, adding yet another portfolio to an already heavy workload.For a party that had promised transparency and good governance, the reshuffles were an awkward start.If the cabinet turmoil unsettled Shah's government, it was a much older policy obsession that brought protesters back onto the streets in force.As mayor, Shah had long pushed to clear informal squatter settlements along Kathmandu's rivers. As prime minister, he revived that campaign on a national scale. From April 2026, authorities began dismantling settlements across the Kathmandu Valley and beyond, eventually affecting more than 2,600 families and around 15,000 people, as per Nepal News. The government promised a resettlement plan offering land within a thousand days, but critics, including lawyers and Gen Z activists, argued that families were being removed before their status as genuine landless squatters had even been verified. Some took the matter to the Supreme Court.Families moved to temporary holding centres were told to leave by July 6, but dozens refused, saying they had nowhere else to go. Days later, monsoon floods struck a holding centre in Kirtipur, forcing the emergency evacuation of around 150 displaced people. When young activists went to check on conditions there, police baton-charged and arrested several of them, a response that drew sharp criticism from opposition figures, including Nepali Congress president Gagan Thapa.It was against this backdrop that Ganesh Nepali took his own life. He had been driving for a ride-hailing app when municipal police locked his motorcycle's wheel over a parking violation. Unable to pay the fine, he set himself alight outside a government office.His death combined two separate grievances, over housing and over heavy-handed policing, into a single wave of anger. Protesters under banners such as the Joint National Squatters Front and the All Nepal National Free Students' Union took to Kathmandu's streets, demanding Shah's resignation, an end to forced evictions, the release of detained activists, and permanent housing for displaced families.Even tomato farmers joined the chorus of discontent, protesting separately over collapsing prices and what they see as a government more interested in imports than in supporting local growers.What has struck many observers most is not the protests themselves, but Shah's response to them: near total silence. As mayor, he rarely engaged with the press. As prime minister, he has given no interviews and holds no press briefings, preferring occasional, cryptic social media posts.That silence extends to parliament itself. Shah walked out midway through the president's opening address to the new legislature and has been largely absent from sittings since, a habit that has drawn criticism even from some who voted for him.Rabi Lamichhane, the RSP's chairman, chose not to contest the prime ministership himself, partly because of pending corruption cases, and instead welcomed Shah into the party as its public face, the Nepali Times reported. But a recent change to the party's constitution now gives Lamichhane the power to remove the parliamentary leader, meaning Shah, in effect, does not fully control his own party. It is a highly unusual arrangement for a sitting prime minister, and one that has fuelled speculation of a future power struggle between the two men.None of this means Shah's popularity has collapsed. Millions of young Nepalis still see him as a break from a discredited political class, and his government has moved quickly on some fronts, including pursuing corruption cases against former leaders. But the events of the past few months show how difficult it is to translate protest energy into steady governance.Yet the protests unfolding today carry a deeper warning. They suggest that the generation which transformed Nepal's politics has not lowered its expectations simply because its preferred candidate is now in power.The chants that carried Balen Shah to power are now echoing outside his own government.The protesters who once demanded a new Nepal have not abandoned that dream. They have simply turned the same expectations on the man they believed could deliver it. For Balen Shah, the revolution is over. The accountability has just begun.
Article Summary: Balendra "Balen" Shah became Nepal's youngest ever prime minister in March 2026. He rose to power on the back of the 2025 Gen Z uprising, a youth-led revolt that burned down Nepal's parliament and forced a four-time prime minister out of office. Barely a hundred days into office, his administration is now facing the same kind of street pressure that toppled his predecessor.

Article Title: Protests rock Dhaka as minority leaders condemn arrest of Hindu man building 81-ft Lord Ram statue
Article Text:
Pattern of persecution

Poll Vote & Share your view What is your opinion on the potential construction of the Lord Ram statue? It should be built as a symbol of unity. It may provoke further religious tensions. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Minority leaders in Bangladesh on Saturday staged a large protest outside the National press club in Dhaka, condemning the arrest of a young Hindu man, Haridas Chandra Tarani Das, and alleging that the money laundering charges against him were fabricated to stop the construction of an 81-foot Lord Ram statue in Gaibandha district.The demonstration, organised by the Bangladesh Hindu-Buddhist-Christian unity council, brought together leaders from the Hindu, Buddhist and Christian communities, who accused the authorities of targeting religious minorities and demanded Das' immediate release.Speaking to ANI, Manindra Kumar Nath, general secretary of the Bangladesh Hindu-Buddhist-Christian Unity Council, strongly criticised the arrest. "Today, Bangladesh Hindu Buddha Krishnalok Tabarishad organised a demonstration against the arrest of Haridas Chandra Tarani Das. Haridas Chandra Tarani Das was arrested by the government some two or three days ago over the claim that he built a Ram Chandra Devata, Ram Chandra statue in Palashbari. In that case, we cannot accept this sort of arrest of Taroni Das."Nath said the arrest reflected a wider pattern of violence and legal action against minority communities in Bangladesh."You know, from the very beginning of the last two years, different types of arrests and atrocities have happened in Bangladesh. Not only that, you know, 3,000 incidents happened all over Bangladesh in the last year. Out of these, 66 were murdered, and there were so many temples attacked by the fundamentalists. It is undesirable. We cannot accept it."According to protest organisers, Das was arrested by law enforcement authorities before being remanded to judicial custody by a local court. Minority leaders alleged the money laundering case was intended to halt the construction of the proposed Lord Ram statue in Palashbari, Gaibandha.The arrest comes weeks after protests by members of the Hindu community over the reported desecration of an image of Lord Ram during an Islamist demonstration in the same district.Addressing the gathering, senior unity council leader Subrata Chowdhury questioned the circumstances surrounding the incident and urged Bangladesh's interim administration to identify those responsible. "A beautiful environment has been created, an environment of harmony has been established. In such a situation, who are they who have caused this kind of incident to embarrass this government? We want to give an ultimatum to the government to take proper action against this. "He also demanded the immediate release of Das and warned of a wider agitation if action was not taken. "If you do not take proper legal action immediately against those who have insulted my religion, then we will call for a larger movement in Bangladesh." Chowdhury further questioned the decision-making behind Das' arrest.He added that the minority communities would continue their protests if Das remained in custody. "The person who has been imprisoned must be released immediately. If he is not released, the Sanatan (Hindu) community, the Buddhist community, and the Christian community of Bangladesh will build a united movement on the streets in the coming days."The protests come amid continued concerns over the safety of minorities in Bangladesh. On June 23, India also raised the issue, urging Dhaka to act against extremist elements following reports of desecration of Hindu deities.Bangladesh's criminal investigation department (CID) had arrested Haridas on money laundering charges involving alleged suspicious transactions worth Tk 9.35 crore. The agency also claimed he had travelled illegally to India in 2010 and later converted to Islam in 2019, according to local media outlets.The arrest came months after the death of 25-year-old Hindu man Chanchal Bhowmik in Narsingdi, an incident that remains under investigation after CCTV footage raised suspicions of possible foul play.Addressing a media briefing in New Delhi, ministry of external affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said, "We have seen reports from Bangladesh regarding acts of desecration involving Hindu deities and their images, which have sparked protests. We expect the Bangladeshi government to curb the extremists there and guarantee the safety of the minority community."
Article Summary: Minority leaders in Bangladesh staged a large protest outside the National press club in Dhaka. They condemned the arrest of a young Hindu man, Haridas Chandra Tarani Das. They alleged that the money laundering charges against him were fabricated to stop the construction of an 81-foot Lord Ram statue.

Article Title: 500 feared dead as 2 boats with Rohingya refugees capsize
Article Text:
Boats Left Rakhine In Late June Carrying Mostly Rohingya Passengers

Rohingya exodus from Rakhine started in 2017



Two boats carrying more than 500 people may have capsized off Myanmar's coast in recent days, UN agencies said on Thursday, as refugees from the war-torn country make perilous maritime journeys in search of safety and better lives.The two vessels left Myanmar's Rakhine State in late June carrying mostly ethnic minority Rohingya passengers, reportedly including some from refugee camps in Bangladesh, the International Organization for Migration and the UN's refugee agency said in a joint statement, citing preliminary information.More than 500 were feared dead, it said. "While the incidents and casualty figures have yet to be officially confirmed, UNHCR and IOM are gravely concerned by devastating loss of life." Rohingya typically avoid such boat journeys at this time of year when conditions at sea are dangerous. The refugees have no way to safely return to Myanmar, where military that killed thousands of Rohingya in 2017 remains in charge.In the latest incidents, the first boat, with about 250 people on board, lost contact after departure and a second vessel carrying about 280 people was believed to have sunk off Myanmar’s Irrawaddy coast on July 8, the UN agencies said. “These journeys took place outside the regular sailing season, when maritime conditions are typically more hazardous,” the statement said. The Rohingya exodus from Rakhine started in 2017 after the Myanmar military launched an offensive, leading to at least 730,000 seeking shelter in Bangladesh.
Article Summary: Two boats carrying more than 500 people may have capsized off Myanmar's coast in recent days, UN agencies say. Boats left Myanmar's Rakhine State in late June carrying mostly ethnic minority Rohingya passengers. Rohingya typically avoid such boat journeys at this time of year when conditions at sea are dangerous.

Article Title: 'Assassin' of B'desh ex-prez Ziaur Rehman held after 45 yrs
Article Text:
Fugitive in Ziaur Rahman assassination case arrested by Bangladesh detectives

DHAKA: Former Bangladesh army Major Muzaffar Hossain - allegedly one of the masterminds and assassins of PM Tarique Rahman's father and former President Ziaur Rahman - has been arrested after being at large for 45 years.The arrest of Hossain - identified in historical records and case documents as the man who allegedly fired the fatal shots at the President at the Chittagong Circuit House on May 30, 1981 - marks the six-month-old Tarique-led BNP govt's first major breakthrough in its promised pursuit of Ziaur Rahman's assassins.The former officer was arrested from the Banani DOHS area of Dhaka at midnight Wednesday, Dhaka Metropolitan Detective Police said. Govt sources said police, after completing legal formalities, has handed over Hossain to Bangladesh army to complete his pending court martial procedures.In the early hours of May 30, 1981, a group of mid-ranking army officers attacked the circuit house and killed Ziaur Rahman - founder of governing BNP. Hossain and Captain Mosleh Uddin were among the officers directly involved in the assassination, officials claimed.
Article Summary: Former Bangladesh army Major Muzaffar Hossain arrested after 45 years. He was allegedly one of the masterminds and assassins of PM Tarique Rahman's father and former President Ziaur Rahman. Arrest marks the six-month-old Tarique-led BNP govt's first major breakthrough in its promised pursuit of the assassins.

Article Title: At least 500 Rohingya feared dead after two boats capsize in Bay of Bengal
Article Text:
According to a statement from United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, the two boats had left Myanmar's Rakhine state in late June carrying mostly Rohingya passengers.

At least 500 people are feared dead after two boats carrying Myanmar's Rohingya minority capsized in the bay of Bengal.According to a statement from the International Organisation for Migration and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, the two boats had left Myanmar's Rakhine state in late June carrying mostly Rohingya passengers, including some who had traveled from refugee camps across the border in Bangladesh.One boat, believed to have been carrying around 250 people, lost contact shortly after departure. A second boat, reportedly carrying 280 people, is believed to have sunk off Myanmar’s Ayeyarwady coast on July 8.″While the incidents and casualty figures have yet to be officially confirmed, UNHCR and IOM are gravely concerned by the potentially devastating loss of life,” the agencies said.The Rohingya, who have fled Myanmar and the overcrowded refugee camps in Bangladesh in large numbers in recent years, usually avoid sea crossings during the monsoon season, when rough weather makes the journey especially dangerous. The UNHCR and the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said recent torrential rain and flooding across the region would have made such voyages even riskier.Around 1.2 million stateless Rohingya, most of them Muslims, remain confined to overcrowded refugee camps in Bangladesh after fleeing waves of violence by Myanmar's security forces.The refugees have no safe route back to Myanmar, where the military accused by the United States of committing genocide against the Rohingya in 2017 remains in power.Those still living in Myanmar continue to face severe restrictions, with many confined to internment camps.Meanwhile, deep cuts to foreign aid by the United States and other donor countries have led to reduced food rations in Bangladesh's refugee camps. At the same time, fighting between Myanmar's military and an ethnic armed group in Rakhine State has further worsened the crisis.Thousands of Rohingyas have died during these crossings over the years, including babies, children and pregnant women. Rights groups have also accused regional maritime authorities of abandoning Rohingya boats at sea and failing to respond to distress calls.The IOM and UNHCR said the latest suspected tragedy highlights the absence of long-term solutions for the Rohingya crisis and urged the international community to step up support for refugees in Bangladesh."Stronger regional and international efforts are needed to prevent further loss of life along one of the world's deadliest maritime routes, including through enhanced search and rescue efforts, access to asylum and protection, and actions against smuggling and trafficking networks," the agencies said.According to the UNHCR, more than 6,500 Rohingya attempted to flee by sea in 2025, while nearly 900 were reported dead or missing, making it the deadliest year on record for Rohingya maritime journeys. The agency said the route now has the highest mortality rate of any major refugee or migrant sea crossing in the world.
Article Summary: Two boats carrying Myanmar's Rohingya minority capsized in the bay of Bengal. One boat, believed to have been carrying around 250 people, lost contact shortly after departure. A second boat, reportedly carrying 280 people, is thought to have sunk off Myanmar’s Ayeyarwady coast on July 8.

Article Title: Nepal court jails ex-deputy PM, home minister in fake refugee scam; 14 others convicted
Article Text: A Kathmandu court has sentenced two former Nepal ministers and 14 others to prison after convicting them in a case involving the alleged creation of fake documents. The documents were reportedly used to help Nepali citizens secure resettlement in the United States by falsely presenting them as Bhutanese refugees, according to court records and lawyers.According to Reuters, former deputy prime minister and energy minister Top Bahadur Rayamajhi was handed a four-year jail term after being found guilty of offences including fraud, crimes against the state and involvement in organised crime. Former home minister Bal Krishna Khand received a two-year sentence for his role as an accomplice, a court document showed.The Kathmandu district court issued the verdicts late on Tuesday. Rayamajhi is currently in custody, while Khand remains out on bail. Both former ministers have denied any involvement in the case.Rayamajhi’s lawyer Dharma Raj Regmi said his client was not involved in decisions related to refugee policy and would challenge the ruling. “He was never involved in policy making for the refugees,” Regmi said, adding that an appeal would be filed.Khand’s lawyer Pankaj Karna also confirmed that he would move an appeal against the verdict.The court also convicted 14 other accused, including a former senior official of Nepal’s home ministry and a former leader representing Bhutanese refugees. They were sentenced to prison terms of up to four years, according to the court document.The investigation into the alleged scam began in 2023, when authorities uncovered claims that Nepali citizens were being falsely presented as Bhutanese refugees to gain access to a US-led third-country resettlement programme. It has not been confirmed whether any individuals obtained resettlement in the US through the alleged scheme.The case is tied to the decades-old Bhutanese refugee crisis, during which around 1,20,000 people of Nepali origin left Bhutan for Nepal from the early 1990s after disputes over citizenship, identity and political rights.Under a resettlement initiative launched after Nepal and Bhutan failed to resolve the issue through repatriation talks, nearly 113,000 Bhutanese refugees were relocated to countries including the US, Canada and Australia. Washington accepted around 100,000 refugees from Nepal, while several thousand remain in camps in eastern Nepal.The court ruling comes amid renewed focus on corruption in Nepal following last year’s youth-led protests that brought down the previous government.
Article Summary: Former deputy prime minister and energy minister Top Bahadur Rayamajhi was handed a four-year jail term. Former home minister Bal Krishna Khand received a two-year sentence for his role as an accomplice. The court also convicted 14 other accused, including a former senior official of Nepal’s home ministry and a former leader representing Bhutanese refugees.
